maintopic: VISIT TO SAINT JOHN, N.B., BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
VISIT TO SAINT JOHN, N.B., BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege I should like to draw to the attention of the house for a few minutes the very informative and highly enjoyable trip a group of us were privileged to make to the city of Saint John.
We live in a wide and large country indeed. In our younger days we all had to memorize facts and figures about the other cities and provinces of our great country. During the last war some of us were able to pay short visits to, or at least go through most of, the provinces of Canada, but of course we saw them only in the dark and sombre attire of war. The need of first-hand knowledge, the need to know better our sister cities and provinces, is constant.
Our short stay in Saint John was indeed a revelation to many and a most enjoyable experience to all. To be shown the actual efforts, to see for ourselves the concrete achievements, to witness the possibilities of the future, and to hear the enthusiastic and genuine professions of faith of the people of Saint John in their proud city which their meticulous and gracious hospitality has so endeared' to us, is certainly an occasion worthy of mention in this house. I know I speak for the entire group when I say we are genuinely grateful to our congenial and devoted friend and fellow member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) for his kind invitation to visit his city. We and our wives were very proud to be part of the Dan Riley flock for the week end. More attentive and efficient direction I am sure would not have been possible.
Our sincere and deep gratitude is also unreservedly extended to the Saint John board of trade, our gracious host in the city. With complete disregard of themselves, the members of that organization made available generous accommodation and carried out elaborate arrangements to ensure to us a most enjoyable stay, giving us the opportunity to learn a great deal about them and get to know them better. We are particularly indebted to the president and his charming wife, Mr. and Mrs. Wasson. We wish to
thank His Honour Lieutenant Governor MacLaren for his highly appreciated hospitality and his spirited and most enjoyable company; also the government of New Brunswick and its popular premier, Mr. McNair, for their complimentary entertainment and kind hospitality, as well as His Worship Mayor George E. Howard and his lady. Our gratitude is also extended to Mr. Crump and his company for the 'concern and courtesy shown us all through the trip and particularly for their grand and unique hospitality on the proud Empress of Canada. We salute Captain Dobson.
Our thanks also go to the Saint John Dry-dock Company Limited and Saint John Marine Transport Limited for the opportunity they gave us to view the city and the harbour from the sea. We also extend our thanks to Senator McLean and Mr. Brennan, to the various industries of Saint John, to the various devoted committees and all those who made their facilities available to us, and finally to all the citizens of that city. It was with a deep sense of gratitude that we said au revoir, and it is with the same feeling that we say thank you.

FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe this is the correct place for me to ask for leave to move, seconded

Wheat
by the member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), the adjournment of the house under standing order 31 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the failure of the government to meet the legitimate demands of wheat producers by announcing a final payment of 8.3 cents per bushel for wheat in the five-year pool, when farmers are entitled to a final payment of not less than 25 cents.
In view of a meeting being held in Regina tomorrow by representatives of western agriculture, I believe that this is a matter of urgent importance.

maintopic: FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Standing order No. 31 reads: Leave to make a motion for the adjournment of the house (when made for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance) must be asked after the ordinary daily routine of business (standing order 15) has been concluded and before notices of motions or orders of the day are entered upon.
I have a recollection that last year I made a ruling that the motion should be made after questions and before the orders of the day are entered upon. However, without deciding definitely upon that, I shall go on with the second paragraph:
The member desiring to make such a motion rises in his place, asks leave to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, and states the matter.
The hon. member has done that.
He then hands a written statement of the matter proposed to be discussed to the speaker, who, if he thinks it in order and of urgent public importance, reads it out and asks whether the member has the leave of the house. If objection is taken, the Speaker requests those members who support the motion to rise in their places and if more than twenty members rise accordingly, the Speaker calls upon the member who has asked for leave.
I must decide whether the motion is in order. There is some doubt as to whether this is the proper time to make such a motion. Without deciding that point I shall allow the motion to stand on this occasion as being in order. I must also decide whether the question is of urgent public importance. My recollection is that when the announcement was made concerning this payment, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) stated there would be ample opportunity to debate this matter when the house went into committee of supply on the supplementary estimates, which he stated would be brought down shortly. If my memory serves me correctly,
I understood the Minister of Finance to say that would be within about ten days, which would be the end of this week or the beginning of next.
The member moving the motion has stated there is to be a meeting in Regina tomorrow.
I do not know the nature of the meeting, but 
even so, it would seem to me this question can be fully discussed in the near future, so it would not come within the rule concerning urgency. I cannot allow the motion to stand.

Arrangements were made by our national employment service to provide transportation at federal government expense between October 1 and December 31 last for 301 men from Newfoundland who volunteered to work in northern Ontario lumber camps. The following orders were placed with the employment service, and the following number of men were dispatched: Great Lakes Paper Company, Fort William, 42 men; Abitibi Power and Paper, Hurkett, 66 men; Brampton Paper Company, 25 men; Marathon Pulp and Paper Company, 44 men; Pineland Pulp and Paper Company, Sudbury, 25 men; Gillies Brothers, Braeside, 50 men; Spruce Falls, Kapuskasing, 49 men, total 301 men. All these companies, Mr. Speaker, are known and recognized as running first-class camps.
The six dissatisfied men mentioned by my hon. friend in his notice are the only men of the 301 who have expressed any dissatisfaction with the working conditions in the camps. Four of them have been placed* to their satisfaction with the Driftwood Timber Company at Hearst, and the remaining two have chosen to return to Newfoundland.
Finally, as to the complaint that no stamps were affixed in the insurance books of these gentlemen, I may say that they had been working for companies that complied with regulation 14 of the unemployment insurance contribution regulations under which these companies have chosen to pay the contributions by bulk payments at specified periods determined by the commission.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the appropriate section under which to make any general observations concerning the measure now before us. I wish to speak to some aspects of the bill generally, and particularly in regard to some of those which have already been discussed and which I hoped might have been amended by the government as a result of that discussion.
One of the things I should like to emphasize in regard to this measure is a point I had hoped would appeal to the Prime Minister, particularly in view of the explanation he gave of the emergency powers bill. When that measure was before us he explained that while it contained many of the provisions appearing in the War Measures Act, it was not deemed advisable to create the impression in the minds of the Canadian people that we have yet reached the stage where we should regard ourselves as being in a state of war. I indicated my support of that view. I said on that occasion that I thought the more it


was possible to emphasize in the minds of the people of Canada that our efforts are directed toward peace, the better it would be in carrying out the work we have under way.
This bill, instead of following the idea put forward by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) at that time, deals with the production of defence materials in a way that goes beyond the powers conferred upon the minister responsible for defence production at the height of the last war. Reference has been made already to a number of the provisions of this bill which go very far and which it will perhaps be more appropriate to discuss when we are dealing with the individual sections. I would point out, however, that this bill goes very much farther than the munitions and supply act. It confers upon the minister as the minister, and not limited to cases in which he has the approval of the governor in council, powers which extend to some of the most important aspects of the Canadian economy.
I would suggest, as others suggested when the bill was up for second reading, that at a time when we are seeking to preserve all the desirable features of democracy it is most desirable that we make sure that we preserve democracy within parliament itself where the final test of our whole democratic system is going to take place. After all, democracy is something which affects every one of the fourteen million people of Canada; democracy is something that is shared by every one of those fourteen million people, but in the end, so far as national activities are concerned, the ability of all those people to express themselves within the democracy is through the channels afforded here in the parliament of Canada. For that reason it has been urged by others as well as by myself that we should not, at a time like this, proceed to extend these extremely wide powers, particularly without any explanation being given as to why such vast powers are necessary at this time.
This is not a subject that is coming up for discussion today for the first time; it has been under consideration for many years by people who are concerned about the preservation of parliamentary democracy. As the members of this house well know, one of the most learned books on that subject was written by Lord Hewart of Bury in 1929 under the title of "The New Despotism." Lord Hewart referred to the great danger of losing real democracy by the extension of what we have come to describe as administrative law into those fields which can still be dealt with adequately by parliament itself.

Lord Hewart did accept the proposition that there are many cases in which administrative law is necessary so that there is from day to day that measure of flexibility which is necessary for strictly administrative acts. He emphasized, however, his own point of view, and the point of view of many great constitutional lawyers of Britain, that where so-called administrative law gives to the government or to an individual minister the power to make decisions which have the effect of law, actually you are denying the responsibility of parliament itself and the rights of parliament in dealing with matters of public concern. At page 35 he had this to say:
Between the rule of law and what Is called "administrative law" (happily there is no English name for it) there is the sharpest possible contrast. One is substantially the opposite of the other.
He then goes on to explain the difference between administrative law and the rule of law under our system of parliamentary government. In referring to the administrative law of France he had this to say:
It is a system which is fundamentally opposed to the English conception of the rule of law, especially as regards exemption from the jurisdiction of the ordinary legal tribunals, in the case of public officials acting in performance or purported performance of their official duties.
He then goes on to make an extended examination of the way in which the extension of legislative authority, without supervision by parliament at the time the decision is made, does in fact challenge the authority of parliament itself where it is something that affects the welfare of the people and creates new regulations, new laws, new activities not contemplated by parliament in any decision they have made.
The whole idea of the making and enforcement of law was dealt with long ago by one of the greatest exponents of our system of law, Sir William Blackstone, in these words:
Where the right of making and enforcing law is vested in the same man, or one of the same body of men, there can be no public liberty.
In this particular bill, not only is authority conferred upon the minister to do certain things which would have a profound effect upon our economy and the life of the whole country over very broad fields1-in fact over almost limitless fields-but we find it contains provisions which make it possible for the minister to delegate that authority to anyone whom he chooses, without any formal approval by the government by order in council. Then we have again the statement by Lord Hewart, to whom I have referred, to be found in the book from which I have already quoted, who says that powers of this kind continue to extend themselves to the 80709-571
Defence Production Act point where we no longer have real democracy, no matter what the form may be. I quote his exact words:
Arbitrary power is certain in the long run to become despotism and there is danger that if this so-called "administrative law" (by government agencies), which is essentially lawless, is gradually extended, it will mean the loss of those hardly won liberties which it has taken centuries to establish.
The proposition I put forward when this bill was up for second reading, the proposition I put forward now, is that when we are already engaged in a world-wide struggle to preserve our traditional system of democracy, that is the time we should most jealously guard those traditions and principles upon which that democracy has been built. Without going into many of the sections in detail I would point out that there are powers in this bill which at no time during the course of the war existed in statutory form in any measure brought forward by the government. We are still waiting for an explanation as to why this power should be given, particularly at the very time the Prime Minister, in discussing another bill, points out that it is desirable for us to refrain from extending powers to the full extent that would be done in time of a general war, because the very act of doing this might in itself convey the impression to the public mind that the government regards this country as already in a state of general war.
Fort that reason I am repeating to the Prime Minister-and I emphasize, to the Prime Minister-my suggestion that in consistency, having regard to what he said in relation to the other bill before the house, this legislation should not confer still wider powers than were conferred during the war, either upon the government or upon a minister; but rather at this stage the government should voluntarily redraft this bill so that the principle of the rule of law would be clearly settled, and the acts done under this legislation would be subject to those ordinary safeguards which are traditional under our system of democracy.

speechtext:
The hon. leader of the opposition having appealed two or three times to the Prime Minister in connection with the terms of this bill, I think I should make a few observations. There is no contention being put before the house that the legislature of the province of Ontario was wrong in enacting the terms of the hydroelectric bill just cited. It is referred to just as an

illustration of the fact that there are occasions when this doctrine that Lord Hewart expounded so eloquently in the book from which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has cited just does not apply to the facts of the kind of life we live in this age and in this world in which we are living. One illustration of the necessity of having something else that will work in a different manner is to be found in the provisions put in this Ontario hydroelectric bill. I do not know that there could be found anyone anywhere, here or in the province of Ontario, to assert that there had happened any of the terrible things that could be conceived of under broad legislation of this kind. Usually, persons who are charged with the responsibility of administering an organization like the Ontario hydroelectric system are reasonable people who discharge their responsibility in a reasonable fashion; and although they might have extremely wide powers to deal with the situation in such a manner as would involve serious inconvenience to a large section of the public, they exercise the discretion that is conferred upon them in a manner that, so far, seems to have given satisfaction to the Ontario public. But it is one of those cases where it is necessary, in order to have a situation that can be handled with efficiency, to have extremely broad powers.
That statute provides that there will be no action without the authorization of the attorney general, without what we refer to as the fiat, something which has existed up to the present time in connection with the administration of federal affairs but which we announced in the speech from the throne we were going to do away with at this session. The government announced its intention of recommending doing away with that old and time-honoured doctrine that there should be no suit against the crown or its agent without a special fiat. I hope it is going to be done away with. It is to be found also in this Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission Act. Possibly after we shall have had some experience with the abolition of the fiat here, it will be abolished elsewhere. I think there are some provinces which have already abolished it and which have had no disagreeable experience as a result of doing so. It is possible that the legislators succeeding my hon. friend in the legislature of Ontario will come to the conclusion that it is not necessary to preserve a provision such as that; but it is there now. Then there is this other thing, that anything done by the commission or by its servants or agents or anything done by a municipality, its servants or agents or anything done by a local commission or its servants or agents, to take care of what

they themselves declare to be an emergency, will give rise to no action before the courts. One could conceive that it would be possible, under the terms of that kind of legislation, for a commission to make an improper declaration of emergency and to use that improper declaration of emergency for improper entry upon the lands or premises of the individual and then deny him any recourse to the courts for the damages resulting from the improper declaration of emergency and the improper entry upon his premises. But the legislature of Ontario did not feel that that was apt to happen, and the hon. member himself did not feel that that was apt to happen, with the kind of commissioners he was going to choose or who would be chosen by his successors; and I do not think it has happened. I am quite sure that after the experience that has been had in this country there are not many who feel that wide provisions in an act of this kind are going to be the occasion of abuse. You can conceive of the possibility of abuse being made of wide powers, but there are not apt to be abuses; and it is apt to be necessary to have the powers to do these things in proper cases, and to leave that to the good judgment, honesty of purpose, experience and knowledge of those who are charged with administering the act.
When we are dealing with some of the sections of this bill it may be that suggestions will be made that they should be toned down or that they should be sharpened up. But here we are dealing with the principle of there being a bill which provides that there may be, under present conditions, powers that are not normally exercised in peacetime. The leader of the opposition, in discussing it on second reading, complained of section 5. When we come to section 5, it will be discussed; but that is the section which provides that the minister may empower someone to do any specific act that he himself could do. The hon. member speaks of the rule of law. That is now the rule of law under the bill which was adopted at the last session of parliament. It was taken textually from the bill which was adopted by this house at the last session of parliament.

speechtext: Which bill is that?

It is the Essential Materials (Defence) Act. Section 5 is an almost verbatim reproduction of the clause in the Essential Materials (Defence) Act which is to be repealed if and when this act comes into force.
The other complaint was that the minister may remove any members, directors or officers of a corporation acting under him. Must he not have the responsibility to this
Defence Production Act house, not only for his personal acts but for the acts that will be performed by those corporations that he may cause to be incorporated to carry out some of the duties that would devolve upon him under this act? Must he not be the one responsible to this house? Is it not our experience that the one who has control of these corporations is the one we look upon as being responsible to this house for the proper administration of those corporations? If there was someone doing things for which he cannot take responsibility before this house, why should he not have the power of replacing him by someone for whose conduct he can assume responsibility before the house?
There are other sections, when we come to them, the language of which may be subject to some discussion; but for the present, the only question is this: Are we in times and in a world where there is occasion for the existence of powers which are not normally exercised in peacetime and about which there was this learned dissertation by Lord Hewart in the book to which the hon. member has referred? The hon. member is right in saying that section 71 of the Ontario hydro electric statute, which was referred to by the minister, is to apply to an emergency, but is to apply when the commission says there is an emergency; and that there were extraordinary powers which, when the commission said there was an emergency, could be exercised. That is something that does not fall under the general rule of law. The commissioners themselves are the ones empowered to make the definite finding that there is the emergency calling for the exercise of the powers, and that is something which it is found to be desirable to have in that kind of set-up. Well, are we not at the present time, when facing our great rearmament problem with our associates in the North Atlantic treaty, in a situation where we have to entrust more than ordinary powers to some public officials to discharge properly and promptly the obligations we have assumed to build up as rapidly as possible the joint strength of these North Atlantic treaty powers?
Once more, when each of these clauses has been reached its language will be looked at very carefully; but I cannot acquiesce in the invitation of the leader of the opposition to say to my colleagues: We will withdraw this bill and bring in some other kind of bill. We feel this is the kind of bill that the circumstances require.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
To follow this through, Mr. Chairman, and in the same spirit in which the Prime Minister has approached this bill, I recognize that there may be a great deal of difference of opinion as to how the

Defence Production Act emergency provision, or the emergency situation, is to be dealt with, and the extent to which legislation should go. I am going to make certain suggestions to the Prime Minister in the hope that they may perhaps be worthy of consideration now or at some future time.
I want to say this: To the extent that there may have been any heat displayed in the earlier remarks, I think it is unfair and unjust to impute improper motives to those who did express the opinion that this is very dangerous legislation. Whether that is right, or whether it is wrong, it is my conviction that it is; and I certainly do resent the statement of the minister which in an indirect way may imply that there was hypocrisy in the presentation of that. But I am going to leave that and come to the clear expression of opinion of the Prime Minister as to his views in regard to this legislation as it is now before us.
I would point out one thing that does affect my own opinion in regard to this, and that, for instance, is the very section 5 to which the Prime Minister has referred. Section 5 of this bill is not in the same wording as the similar provision in the Essential Materials (Defence) Act, the section that we will consider in detail. Section 5 reads as follows:
The minister may authorize any person, on his behalf and under his control and direction, to do any act or thing or to exercise any power that the minister may do or exercise under this act.
Whereas in the Essential Materials (Defence) Act, section 5, subsection (2) reads:
The minister may authorize persons to act under his control and direction on his behalf in the exercise of powers conferred on him by this act, or by regulation.
There is, as the Prime Minister will see, a very clear distinction between the two. One is to exercise powers conferred upon the minister under the direction of the minister, and the other is power to delegate authority; but we can discuss that when we come to that section.
I believe that we have before us an issue that goes beyond the actual wording of this bill, and one which we should consider, whether it be at this time or at some other time.
I think it was the consensus in this house, from what I can read of the discussions at the time, that it was desirable after the end of the last war that the extensive controls and very wide and sweeping controls which were set up during the war should be relaxed as fast as they conveniently could be, consistently with the general welfare of the people of Canada. Now, unexpectedly we
[Mr. Drew.)

find ourselves adopting measures that confer powers that are not only as wide as, but in many cases much wider than, those taken over by the government as the result of the decision of parliament during the time of war itself.
This is a subject which has been under consideration for a long time. I think hon. members should be considering how we are to retain parliamentary democracy and at the same time place in the hands of this government power to do not only these things that ordinarily can only be done as a result of decision by parliament, but also to do things which would not ordinarily be within the jurisdiction of the dominion government at all.
It has been made quite clear that as a result of the emergency which we have now entered it is necessary for the dominion government to have powers to do certain things that ordinarily would be within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. The passing of a bill of this kind therefore not only withdraws from the members of parliament their discretion and their judgment in regard to extremely important steps that will be taken, but it may also withdraw from the provincial legislatures and the provincial governments control and authority over things that it was intended they should control when our basic written constitution was adopted in 1867.
If it is necessary to proceed with bills of this nature, and to enact laws which will give such sweeping powers, then I suggest the time has come for us to face the necessity of some new device by which there will be a continuing supervision over the activities of government and the activities of ministers under bills of this kind. How that is to be done I do not propose to suggest in detail at the moment, but I would suggest that perhaps we might learn something from what has been done in France for a great many years.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Hold more frequent elections.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
No, this does not refer to that
aspect of their constitutional organization. I was just going to say that no matter what our admiration may be for the people of France-and it is very great-nevertheless we would not wish to find ourselves in a position similar to that in which they constantly find themselves as far as elections and forming governments are concerned.
For some considerable time, and quite a long time before the adoption of the present constitution, the French constitution of the day did establish the practice of administrative law, with dictates by governments very similar to those which we are now providing for in legislation of this kind. While I

think there are ways in which their constitution should be improved-and we would all hope that it will be improved for the greater stability of government in France in these critical days-nevertheless there are also some things which we can learn from them in regard to different aspects of their handling of their own affairs.
The step that they took to meet the situation arising from the conferring of administrative powers of this kind upon the government was to set up what they called the council of state. The council of state is a large appointed body with perhaps a hundred members, from time to time having different groups within that council set up to deal with different problems arising from this system of adminstrative law and related law.
That council of state, and particularly some of the bodies set up under it, have functions at times similar to those of the privy council. They have at times even wider powers, because they can review this administrative legislation and pass judgment upon whether it is in keeping with the general welfare of the people. I am not saying that we can or should adopt something exactly similar to the council of state of France, but I am pointing out that for many long years it has been recognized in France that when you take away from the elected representatives of the people the responsibilities over administrative legislation which will have a tremendous and profound effect upon the general activities and welfare of the people, there should be some mechanism which exercises some measure of supervision over that type of law which has been regarded as so dangerous by so great an expert as Lord Hewart of Bury, and by others with similar experience in the constitutional field. I suggest that, in consultation with the provinces, in the light of events which have emerged in the last few months, the desirability of setting up some body with special judicial authority, so that some of the dangers of administrative law of this type may be removed, would be highly desirable, and particularly at a time when we are seeking to preserve the full strength of our democratic system.
I am putting this forward now because it seems to me it is appropriate to offer the suggestion at a time when we have under consideration a bill which carries administrative law as far as this bill carries it. Whether the Prime Minister feels that this is the time to consider a suggestion of that kind or not, in any event I recognize that this would be something outside the scope of the bill itself. However, as we consider this subject, and as it appears clear that the government proposes to proceed with the bill, which contains these very wide powers, without defining 80709-58
Defence Production Act clearly the field in which those powers may be exercised, I would hope consideration would be given to the initiation of discussions which might lead to the setting up of some independent body, judicial or semi-judicial, which might act in a supervisory and advisory capacity, as well as having certain clearly defined and limited judicial responsibilities in regard to legislation of this kind.

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? We have gone through this administrative law process once before within my recollection. The process now is watered down compared to what it was in the original emergency powers measure. Would the hon. member say in what respect either the individual or the provinces were permanently affected by the process we went through as a result of legislative acts?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I would say that what happened was this:	Under the emergency powers
legislation so many powers were taken over by the dominion government that the provincial governments had no choice but to carry forward the agreements. They were clearly stated to be temporary agreements, as the hon. member will recall because, as I remember, he was a member of the government in Ontario at the time the original agreements were signed under which certain taxing powers of the provinces were handed over-and very freely handed over- as part of the general attempt to increase the authority of the dominion government in regard to certain aspects of the preparation for war.
But as will be recalled, those agreements did not prove to be temporary at all. They were renewed; and now apparently we are to see an extension of those agreements still further. My own opinion is that the extent to which agreements of that kind have gone, agreements under which fixed amounts of money were to be received in return for ordinary taxing powers the provinces were intended to have under the constitution, is the direct result of the exercise of that power during the period of war. I should think a committee such as I have mentioned, one having functions somewhat similar to those of the council of state in France, would be likely to examine situations of that kind, and make it easier to protect the relationship between dominion and provincial governments, where it is necessary for the dominion government to exercise powers which do encroach upon ordinary provincial jurisdiction.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, having spoken at some length in the debate on second reading, I certainly do not intend to take the time of the committee

Defence Production Act for more than, a few minutes now. However, there are one or two points I should like to make.
In the first place, so that there may be no misunderstanding as to my feelings, I should like to quote one sentence I used at the beginning of my speech the other night when I said:
In the first place, I should like to say what I think we all feel, namely, that defence production must not be delayed.
And then I said:
We must not allow private interests to stand in the way of defence measures.
I should like to make that perfectly clear, and it applies to anything I shall say. My only reason for taking the time of the committee is that the more I thought about it over the week end the more deeply concerned I became about the fact that, apparently, we are drifting into the giving of these powers. So far as I can see, we are doing it very lightly. I think there is nothing more undesirable than to give powers which in themselves are unwise merely because we think, or because it is thought, that they will be well used by the person who exercises them. When you get down to it, that seems to be the only argument made. Let me point out that we are giving these immense powers for an indefinite time. They are not being given in wartime when there is a natural end; they are being given when they may be continued indefinitely.
We are also being asked-and this is the thing I differ with so strongly-we are being asked to consider this on the basis that these powers are just as essential as they were in wartime. I shall not take the time of the committee to do more than reiterate that I believe the similarity between the minister's job now and the job in wartime is entirely superficial, and that the dissimilarity is far greater. I believe there is no real similarity at all.
The other evening I raised another question concerning the provisions of section 16, which appears to be the financial section in the bill. I do not wish to take myself too seriously, and I would not expect the minister to take me too seriously, but I have thought that one might have had some explanation as to why what I suggested could not be done. I did not offer the suggestion without having discussed it with some people- several people, in fact, who I believe have some knowledge of government; and they were not members of my own party, may I say. The suggestion I put forward, in a very tentative way, seemed to me to be good common sense. However, no notice has been taken of it at all. There may be when we reach the discussion of the sections, but none


has been up to this time. It seems to me the minister merely reiterates that he must have the bill, the whole bill and nothing but the bill.
The Prime Minister, I am glad to see, made a disarming speech a few moments ago in which he suggested that we may be able to deal with this on its merits. But my view is that I do not think we can deal with it on its merits if the whole background of the bill is that we must assume that these powers, with only very minor adjustments, are necessary. The powers, it seems to me, are almost unlimited; I can find no limitation in them. Certainly there is no substantial limit -and they go on for an indefinite period.
I shall not take more of the time of the committee. I do hope, having regard to what the Prime Minister said, that we may be able to look at this without, as I say, being faced with the proposition that the powers have to be given virtually in their entirety.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to obtain information as to the relationship between the powers under this bill and those given under the emergency powers bill, with respect to possible price controls.
When we were dealing with the emergency powers bill I believe it was the Minister of Justice who made it clear that that bill did include powers to impose price controls, if the government decided to take that action. The bill now before us, among other things, will repeal the Essential Materials (Defence) Act which was passed last fall. The Prime Minister drew our attention to that a moment ago.
The Minister of Justice, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and others will recall that when we were discussing the Essential Materials (Defence) Act last fall it came out that the provisions of that bill gave the minister in charge, namely the Minister of Trade and Commerce, power to establish controls with respect to essential materials; and essential materials were defined as those materials involved in the defence program. I tried to pin him down at the time to certain specified items1-I notice the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) is smiling; he remembers the occasion, I am sure-such as steel, and it was admitted that under the provisions of the Essential Materials (Defence) Act, if steel got into short supply because of defence purchases, the Minister of Trade and Commerce would be able to control the price of steel. I tried to go on to meat and suggested that if purchases of meat for the armed forces had the same effect, the same result might follow. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said that that might be permitted by the act

but that so far as his intentions were concerned he simply wanted control under that act over those things which related to matters directly connected with the defence effort.
The Essential Materials (Defence) Act is being repealed by this bill. From what has been suggested and from looking over the bill itself I take it that the essential features of the Essential Materials (Defence) Act are being carried forward into this legislation. For example, under this bill it will be possible to declare certain materials essential for the purposes of defence, and that having been done it will be within the authority of the government or of the minister to appoint controllers and do anything that may be deemed necessary in order to conserve those materials, to facilitate their production and so on.
It seems to me that it adds up to this: There is granted by this bill to the minister of defence production the power to impose controls, including price controls, over certain items and certain materials in our economy. So, if what I have said is correct, what we have is two sets of permission. We have permission under the Emergency Powers Act for the government to bring in price controls of as wide a nature as it may choose to bring in. We have the power under this bill for the minister of defence production to establish controls with respect to defence materials.
I will be quite frank and state that my reason for directing attention to this is that we have heard various rumours as to who would be responsible for price controls if they are brought in. There has been a rumour that they would come under the Department of Finance as was the case during the last war. There has been another rumour that this time they will come under the department of defence production. It has been suggested in another rumour that if we do get controls they will start with defence materials. That seems to be consistent with the provisions of the Essential Materials (Defence) Act which are being carried forward into this bill.
I should like to know if the Prime Minister can tell us what the plan is if the government does respond to the demand for price controls. The Prime Minister knows the arguments that I have put forward repeatedly for price controls. I am not trying to ask him a leading question on that matter. Just at the moment I am trying to get this confusion straightened out. If we do get controls will they be administered under some other department such as the Department of Finance or will they come under the aegis of the minister of defence production?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: If control is needed of materials declared to be essential for war purposes, those controls might be exercised under this bill. But this bill would not allow the establishment of controls that would extend to commodities. For instance, there might be a control over steel, but this bill would not allow a control over the prices of automobiles or other articles manufactured from steel. If there is to be any system of controls of a substantial extent, controls over any wide field, that would have to be done by virtue of regulations or orders made under the Emergency Powers Act. This bill would allow limited regulations to be made affecting the allocation and distribution of materials.

speechtext: Basic materials.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Basic materials. But it would not permit the control and allocation of commodities. With the act that was passed last September we were proceeding on the theory that we did not have to rely upon an emergency that would displace jurisdiction, but that we could exercise certain controls over those materials that might be shortened in supply by the requirements of defence as something necessarily incidental to the proper organizing of defence. Now we are asking parliament to declare that there is the kind of emergency that authorizes the displacement of jurisdiction. If there was to be an interference with the free flow of our economy, that would come under the Emergency Powers Act; whilst if there were merely to be the control and allocation and distribution of materials declared by the governor in council to be essential for war purposes, that could be done by regulation under this defence production act.
There would not be any attempt under the act with respect to the department of defence production to establish any general system of controls over the sale and distribution of commodities in Canada.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
That seems to me to be
rather confusing. From what the Prime Minister has said it would appear that the government contemplates setting up a dual system of controls. The Prime Minister has referred specifically to the Essential Materials (Defence) Act of 1950 and it seems to me that under that act price controls could be exercised over those things that enter into defence preparedness, but which would have an effect on the whole economy.
I was looking up some statistics today and I find that the price index of eight essential supplies used on western farms has increased from 128 in August, 1946, to 194 in February 1 of this year, an increase of 66 points. We are anxious that this tremendous increase,

Defence Production Act not only in the cost of living but in the cost of production which affects everybody engaged in production, should be brought under some control. My understanding of this bill was that when taken in conjunction with other bills we have passed there would be no question of the government having the right to exercise that control.
What I am afraid of is that there will be some dual system of controls which may result in ineffectiveness and a great deal of confusion, both to the persons who are using supplies and to the consumers and other purchasers who are using those supplies that might be put under some control by these pieces of legislation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: During the last war there were differences, as there necessarily had to be. Some things can be distributed by a system of rationing, by coupons. Other things have to be distributed by direct permits granted because of the special conditions in which the applicant for the permit may be placed. For instance, there was the control of building. It was not by a system of coupons that gave everyone the right to do a certain restricted amount of building. A special permit was authorized for a special building upon presentation of the facts and circumstances surrounding the application for that permit. I have no doubt that if we had an extensive system of control there would have to be the same distinction again. There are certain things for which each individual should have a coupon or permit which would entitle him to a limited quantity. Other things, however, are required only by a relatively small portion of the population, and there you cannot have a uniform system of coupons to everybody. You must have a special examination of the circumstances under which a permit is applied for. So I have no doubt that a dual system of that kind would have to be applied in any method of controlling the distribution of short supplies.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I think I grasp the Prime Minister's point, and 1 can understand the difficulties,

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES

I would not want to
promise the house that if we ran up against something where the courts said this was not good enough we would not come back to parliament; if we thought it should be done, we would ask parliament to authorize it; but I think the law officers have drawn this in language that should be sufficient to cover all the enabling powers apt to be required.

permit me, I do not think he should say this is a total-war measure. This is a part of the measures being taken by this country and eleven other nations banded together to try to prevent war.
