subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I do not mind the Prime Minister rising on all the questions of privilege he wishes, but he has just been popping up and interrupting. It is quite clear that the cabinet have put into this bill all the powers they believe would be required in the event of a war. Perhaps the Prime Minister will agree that is fairly put. That is all I have had in mind throughout. Now, such was not the case with regard to the Emergency Powers Act. We believe that if the government is following one policy with regard to the-Emergency Powers Act, it should follow a, similar policy in the Defence Production Act. Rather than take what I describe as full!

Defence Production Act wartime powers, it should bring in a bill similar in nature to the Emergency Powers Act, but of course dealing with a different subject.
On Friday last I suggested that the powers contained in the bill which are for wartime, as distinct from the powers needed at the moment, should either be deleted from the bill or should only be brought into force by proclamation. There should be a provision in the bill that those particular sections would only be brought into force by proclamation, and in the event of war. Take, for example, the power to seize a man's business. As the Prime Minister knows, there is a power in section 27 which enables the minister to step in and take over a man's business. A few minutes ago the minister admitted that he has had no trouble of that kind to date. I should like to know from the Prime Minister why a provision enabling the minister to take over a man's business, even though that man has no contract with the government, is necessary. That is typical of the type of power which we think is not needed at this time, and should not be placed on the statute books. Can the Prime Minister explain why it is necessary to have power of that kind?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
As I understand it, section 27 is limited to cases where the minister is satisfied that a person who has entered into a defence contract has failed or is likely to fail to perform it. Although this is not actual war, this is an endeavour to procure for the armed forces what they would require to be strong in the event of war, and for the purpose of building up that strength as an aid in preventing aggression.
When we come to the sections, if the hon. member has special comments to make about the language in any of them, they will be listened to. I do not know what the decision upon them will be, but they will be listened to. It is not the desire to have anything that is not considered desirable for the purpose of creating as rapidly as possible a situation which, in the opinion of ourselves and our associates, will make aggression unlikely.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I think the Prime Minister
will find that the government is much more likely to secure good results from the Canadian people as a whole if an endeavour is made to co-operate with them, rather than take such powers as these which, after all, are rather drastic. This is particularly true when there is a strong penalty section in the bill. If a man does not comply with the provisions of the bill, he can be fined or imprisoned. Surely, under present conditions, that should be enough.

With regard to the taking of a man's business, may I point out to the Prime Minister that section 27 contains the power to take over a business firm which has a contract with the government, but there is also power to take over a firm which has been directed by the minister to do work for the government, and where there is no contract at all. There is the power there to step in and take over that man's business, even though only a small part of it may be in use for the production of war materials. Now, powers of that type should not we believe be taken in the present legislation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member will wish to direct his observations to such of these clauses as are, in his opinion, faulty in that way.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Twice during the debate on this bill I have directed a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have asked him if he would be kind enough to tell the members of this house as much as he can about the plans for the production of five specific materials of war which will be dealt with under this bill. They are planes, tanks, guns, vehicles and small arms. A few minutes ago the minister said I had answered my own question on Friday night, implying I believe that the answers were in the speech delivered by the Minister of National Defence. I believe I proved, perhaps to the intense boredom of the house, that the answers to my questions were not contained in the speech by the Minister of National Defence, because that speech does not contain any specific information regarding the production of what I consider to be important materials of war.
I am asking this question in no way to put the minister on the spot, to embarrass him or to make political capital out of it. I am simply asking to learn what the plans of the government are so far, and if they have not gone far enough for the minister to give the information, I would be glad to know that. I am extremely interested in this question, and I believe the people of the country are vitally interested in it. A large amount of their $5 million will go to the production of these things. The minister was kind enough during the earlier stages of the debate to indicate that he would be glad to give the answers to these questions when the bill was before the house. It is my belief that the time to get an answer is when clause 1 is before the committee. If I am wrong, I should like to be told, and I earnestly ask the minister to comply with my request.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
This bill does not refer to the construction of planes, tanks, small arms or

anything else. It provides certain broad powers applying to the whole range of defence contracts. I should like to give to my hon. friend a dissertation on what we are doing on aircraft, tanks and small arms; but to do so would require at least a forty-minute speech. I will probably give a summary when the estimates are before the house. But surely he does not want me to break off this debate, without preparation, and attempt to give all the details of all five products he has asked about; that would constitute a cross-section of a good deal of the defence work that we are doing at the present time. I wish to be reasonable, but that is not a reasonable request on this particular bill.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: It is not that I am asking this question without any warning, Mr. Chairman. I asked this question exactly ten days ago and the minister then said, as reported at page 630 of Hansard of February 23: "I will be glad to make it on the bill." Ten days is quite some time. I can think of no better way of taking up the time of the committee than for the committee to hear the plans to produce these vitally important war materials. The minister has had ten days' warning. He said he would give a report at this time; and I do not think that I am making an unfair request when I ask him to follow through on the undertaking he gave at that time.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: As we go through the bill, if my hon, friend can find an appropriate paragraph which deals with the construction of tanks, planes or guns, we shall stop there and discuss them at that stage.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I think that the minister is not giving the committee or the country credit for the interest in the matter of defence production which the committee and the country in fact have. This section gives the title of the act. It is cited as the Defence Production Act. Surely planes, tanks, guns and vehicles are defence production. Surely what the minister intends to do under this bill is to let contracts; in fact, in some cases, to direct that certain firms produce these materials for defence. I can think of no better place for the minister to tell us the general plans of the department which is now to be set up for the production of defence materials than at this time when we are considering the general clause of this bill to set up a defence production department.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Perhaps the quickest way is to make this the children's hour and discuss these things. In the field of aircraft-to take the first item-we are now in production on the F-86-E aircraft which is the latest version of the F-86 plane. A good many hon. members visited the plant of Canadair where
Defence Production Act this operation is going on. We have arranged for government-furnished equipment at the rate of twenty planes per month; and it is expected that over the next few months that figure will be the production output of the plant. Everything there is I think under control. As soon as our own jet engines are in quantity production and as soon as the supply of g.f.p. can be had in greater volume, that production figure can be stepped up to fifty planes a month if required.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: What is g.f.p?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Government-furnished property. At Malton the CF-100 is coming into production. That is the plane called the Canuck. It is expected that production there will be stepped up to twenty planes a month. Offhand I cannot tell just what month the first plane will be off the assembly line. Of course the prototype has been built and has been tested. The Canuck is expected to be powered with the Orenda engine which has now been thoroughly flight-tested and which will be in quantity production by midsummer.
An agreement has been entered into to produce Harvard trainers. One thousand of them are to be produced for Canadian account and it is expected that a substantial order will be added to that number for United States account. The Harvard is powered with the Wasp engine. Preparations are being made to produce the Wasp engine in Canada so that everything to do with the Harvard aircraft will be a Canadian product. Recently a competition among plane manufacturers has resulted in the de Havilland company submitting the successful prototype and a substantial order for Beaver aircraft is being placed by the United States government with the de Havilland company.
Arrangements are being made for the production of aircraft accessories in this country. We are stepping up the production of magnesium castings and a great variety of products that go into the Orenda engine, into the CF-100 and also into the other aircraft that I have mentioned.
Is that sufficient information on aircraft for my hon. friend, or would he like me to expand on that? I want to be sure and satisfy him this time so that he will not ask this question again.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: That is very good.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
In the matter of tanks we are doing nothing. In the last war we found that Canada was not in a position to produce tanks economically. It is too heavy a drain on our supplies of steel and other products, and we believe that our capacity can be more usefully employed by leaving the building of tanks to the enormous arsenals that were

Defence Production Act built in the United States for that purpose. We will procure our tanks from the United States.
The next item was guns, I think. The gun plant at Sorel, which did such important work during the last war, is engaged in producing a three-inch naval gun of the latest type. It is a large order, largely for the United States, but the Canadian requirements are part of the order. I do not remember the number of guns but it is a contract running into some $30 million. The same plant is also tooling up to build the 155-millimetre gun. It was tooling up for the 105-millimetre gun but that work has been held up, I believe, for possible type changes.
In the field of small arms, the arsenal at Long Branch is tooling up for the gun that is used in the F-86. It is an aircraft gun. I am not sure whether it is a 20-millimetre gun or a * 50-calibre gun. I do not keep all those details in mind. I am not sure just what the program is, but in any case the plant that made the bulk of the small arms in the last war is tooling up for the guns that the army' have ordered and will be in a position to go into production fairly soon.
As I said before, we have not put a rifle into production. The principal reason for that is that no standard rifle has been decided on. Nor has standard rifle ammunition been selected. We have large stocks of the rifle which was used in the last war, and we can readily obtain as many as we like of the Garand rifle, used by the United States. There is not the same urgency in small arms as there is about some other types of production; but as soon as the standard rifle is determined upon we will go into the production of that rifle.
What was my hon. friend's next question?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Vehicles.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
We are tooling up for two types of vehicles; one is the 4x4 and the other is the 6x6. We had intended to tool up for the jeep, but there has been some difficulty in getting manufacturing rights straightened out, with the result that no definite arrangements have been made for the jeep as yet.
My hon. friend will appreciate that failing the outbreak of war the number of vehicles required is not great. The important thing in this circumstance is the tooling rather than the production. It is quite easy to purchase all the vehicles that we need at the present time much more cheaply than by tooling up for them, but we are providing the capacity to produce these three types of vehicles which, it is expected, will pretty well cover the range as far as vehicles for the Canadian army are concerned.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Are these vehicles of the
American type?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: American type.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: All American type?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: One other question. Are we doing anything, for instance, with regard to bazookas or mortars? Are you going to buy them from the United States?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Canadian arsenals are producing both-I do not remember the details. As I say, the Canadian arsenals are producing or preparing to produce anything required by the Canadian army for which they can get any substantial volume or are likely to have any substantial volume in the event of war. Arsenals are making a bazooka. Next, you will ask me if it is a big bazooka or a small one. I cannot tell you. I am speaking here without having made myself familiar with these matters in the last two or three days, but I think my hon. friend will find that the Canadian arsenals are working on the type of weapons they made in the last war. We have one type of arsenal for each type of weapon that was manufactured in the last war. They are all busy; and even in the field of explosives we are doing on a small scale what we did in the last war.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Will the minister permit one question? I understood him to say that they were tooling up for two types of vehicles, though, at the present time, his words were: "We can get out and get what we need more cheaply". Will the minister make that a little clearer? What changes will there be in the circumstances that we will not be able to get them later? Will it be because those who are now manufacturing them will be doing something else, and therefore we must tool up?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I said before that the number of vehicles we require today is small. In other words, an army in training in Canada does not use many vehicles as compared with an army on the march or normally fighting abroad.
What we are creating now is the capacity to produce, which is important. If we had extensive operations abroad we would not be able to buy vehicles we want more cheaply somewhere else. The other sources of supply would be manufacturing at full capacity for the requirements of their own troops. We think it is important to have in this country the capacity to produce these three types of vehicles, and we are pressing to establish that capacity.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: But we are tooling now to produce jeeps, although the manufacturing rights have not been straightened out?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: No, we are not tooling to produce jeeps. We are trying to straighten out the manufacturing rights, and when we do we will start to produce jeeps.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I understood the minister to say we were now getting ready to produce three types.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: No; what I meant to convey was that military plans include production of three types. We are tooling for two types, and we are trying to clear the paths so that we can tool for the third.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Would the minister clear up a question I asked a little earlier? On February 5 the Minister of National Defence made the definite statement that orders for $50 million worth of vehicles had actually been placed. Then on February 23 I had an order for return which stated that only $2,500,000 had been placed. I wonder how the difference is accounted for.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
The Minister of National
Defence said that an amount of $50 million had been allocated for vehicles. Was that not it?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: No; I have his statement here. He said: "During this period orders have been placed for the sum of $701 million."

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: That is, the army, navy and air force had placed orders with the Canadian Commercial Corporation.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: They had been placed with the company?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: With the Canadian Commercial Corporation for $701 million. If the hon. member compares the statement that I gave for orders placed by my department he will find that it does not correspond with the Minister of National Defence's list of orders placed. The latter list means orders placed with the Canadian Commercial Corporation, or allocated.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I see.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I think the $50 million was the amount that was allocated in the defence estimates for vehicles.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
After listening to the last half hour's discussion I feel that the kind of information that we are putting on the record is certainly not necessary or desirable at this time.
A few days ago someone asked the minister if he would name the seven points in Canada that might be vulnerable to an air attack,
Defence Production Act and he immediately said no, he did not think that it was good business to point out to the enemy exactly where he could hit us the hardest. This afternoon we have been drawing a blueprint for the record of exactly what we are going to manufacture and where we are going to manufacture it down to the last detail. I think myself it is bad security technique. However, that is not what I rose to say.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Why did you say it?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I thought that some of the
younger members, with less experience, were taking advantage of the fact that the minister is a bit irritable this afternoon, and provoked him into something that he would not do under ordinary circumstances.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: He is quite normal.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
The responsibility is with the questioners rather than with the man who answered the questions. It was completely inconsistent with the attitude we took a few days ago not to blueprint the vulnerable spots.
What I rose to say was this. The emergency legislation now before the house is not confined completely to what the Minister of Trade and Commerce is getting at this time. In my opinion the whole thing has to be viewed in the light of both bills, namely, the bill the Prime Minister is putting through to take certain emergency powers in the matter of protecting the economy of Canada against inflation and exploitation, and the bill we are now discussing. Both go together. If there were not excessive exploitation you would not have very much inflation. The guy who drives prices sky high is the fellow who creates inflation.
Everybody is much concerned with the Prime Minister's bill. He himself says that it is stand-by legislation, and if and when the government thinks an emergency has come about we will apply it. But most people are afraid that we will not apply it.
We think that he should have applied that legislation long ago. We feel that it should be applied immediately. I refer particularly to price controls to stop runaway inflation.
On the other hand, the minister who has the most difficult job, namely, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, is given the responsibility of organizing the whole economy of Canada in the event of an emergency. When that bill comes before the house the argument is immediately raised that its powers are too sweeping. We must restrict those powers, and so forth. My conception of it is that if a certain department of government is going to be given the serious
S14	HOUSE OF
Defence Production Act responsibility of putting the country on a war footing in the event of an emergency, then we must also give that department the necessary authority to give effect to the program in the event of an emergency. You cannot restrict one and give the other; it has got to be a complete responsibility.
I am not concerned about what the minister will do with it. I do not think he will hurt very much the economy of the country from the standpoint of those who are going to produce, so far as the profit end of the matter is concerned. The only point that does concern me is that we ought not to permit the kind of business that crept in during the last war.
I believe the minister has to have the responsibility for which he asks, because he will be given the task of implementing a program he may have in mind or on paper. He will have to go out and let contracts as he did in 1939 and 1940. But, despite the gravity of the situation of those days, just after Dunkirk, no one in the country who could produce munitions and vehicles of war would produce them unless the profit limitation, then set at 5 per cent, was removed from war contracts.
It was removed, with the result that we established a very bad kind of contract. That was the cost-plus contract, which tended toward waste in all directions, because the more a manufacturer paid out for the completion of a contract the greater were his profits, and the greater was the incentive for waste and abuse. That certainly was true of most of the contracts let on that basis. Take a look at shipbuilding contracts, for example. Costs were terrific. I believe the minister's experience at the time of the last war should be helpful now.
Then there was the matter of accelerated depreciation. Many phrases and terms crept into business transactions during the last war. Depreciation certainly was accelerated. When the minister of finance of that day proceeded to defend accelerated depreciation, stating that he believed it quite justifiable to give the Aluminum Company of Canada $180 million of the taxpayers' money, and to write it off in three years as accelerated depreciation, and stated that he considered it good business -

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I interrupt the hon. member to say that the government gave no money whatever to the Aluminum Company, nor did it lend them money or deliver them money in any shape or form, except to pay so much a pound for the aluminum bought by this government. And the amount of aluminum we bought was trivial compared with the figure stated.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I have heard this matter discussed a good many times, and have read the report of the committee on war expenditures. Th hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar made quite an issue of it and there were special sittings of the committee to deal with the matter. The minister may say that I am wrong technically, but I would ask this question: Did not the government pay the Aluminum Company an additional 2J cents a pound on every pound of aluminum produced?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: No. The government of Canada during the war paid the cheapest price for aluminum obtainable anywhere in the world. We paid nothing extra to them-and neither did the Americans.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Well, it has taken the minister and the government at least eight years to catch up with this argument. I have heard it advanced many times, and it is on the record in a good many places, that $180 million of the taxpayers' money was written off in three years by way of accelerated depreciation.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: For the Canadian Aluminum Company.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: It is entirely mistaken.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I have to accept the minister's word; but I still think that that type of depreciation was allowed many companies across the country, and that it is wrong in principle.
However, the point I am seeking to make is that there were thousands of Canadians who were never in a position to build homes under the national housing scheme. I suggested before, and I repeat my suggestion now, that if I made application under the National Housing Act to build a home which would cost about $10,000-and that is about the term they use-and if I agreed as to the type of house I wanted, in view of what has occurred in other respects I should be permitted to ask for accelerated depreciation, so that I might be allowed in three years to depreciate the total value of the house. In those circumstances I would own the house at the expiration of three years. I made that suggestion before and I was told that it was not good business.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: If you owned a house in which you did not live you could write depreciation on it; but I do not think it would help you very much to write accelerated depreciation.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I am just carrying out the
principle of accelerated depreciation as it was applied to plants all across this country all

during this last war. My suggestion would just carry it a little further: If it is good business in the creation of a plant, then it certainly should be good business in providing homes for our citizens, and particularly those who fought the war for about a couple of dollars a day.
I am not against the power being given the minister in the bill; but when the money of the taxpayers, through accelerated depreciation, has been handed over to companies across the country, either for purposes of expansion or for the building of new plants, the same principle should be carried into the building of homes. In view of his experience during the last war the minister should place some limits on war profits, if and when he puts this legislation to work.	.
I would ask the minister to tell me at this time whether he thinks the government's program is a good one, and whether the expansion of the steel industry is one of the problems to be considered. A few days ago several newspapers, including the Ottawa Citizen and the Ottawa Journal, carried the report of a speech made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the United States, upon which occasion he commented upon the development of the St. Lawrence waterways project. He said-unless he was misquoted- that unless that program is carried through, it would be necessary to shift some of the central steel plants down to the Atlantic seaboard.
Does the minister consider that that would be bad business? Would it be bad to have decentralization of industry in Canada, particularly in connection with the basic steel industry? When he spoke this afternoon the Prime Minister pointed out with some force that most of the program for defence at this time was to be in connection with equipment and arms, and the helping of our allies under the North Atlantic treaty. That presupposes that most of this equipment and production for defence purposes, amounting to $5 billion, will be going to Europe rather than to the Far East.
I ask the minister to realize that the logical place for expansion in steel manufacture to produce materials to be sent to Europe is on the Atlantic seaboard. This would provide the shortest route and save the hauling of basic materials across the country and the hauling back of the finished products. I think it is right that this money should be spent for the purpose of helping our allies under the North Atlantic pact, but serious consideration should be given to producing a lot of that equipment on the Atlantic seaboard.
I have another question to ask because I consider the minister to be perhaps one of
Defence Production Act the best structural engineers in Canada, an engineer with long experience. He will remember that I have discussed on many occasions with the Minister of Transport over the years the completion of the Canso bridge. A total of $250,000 has been spent by the federal government in determining the feasibility of this project. Newfoundland is considered to be one of our outposts in the matter of defence and the possibility is that it will become a fortress in the years that lie ahead. That means that a lot of material will have to be shipped in that direction from central Canada unless there is greater decentralization of industry. Can the minister inform the house as an engineer if that Canso project could not be considered as part of our defence program?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
With regard to my remark in the United States that without the St. Lawrence waterway the steel industry would gradually be forced to move from the great lakes to the Atlantic seaboard, of course that applied to the steel industry as a whole. The steel industry of the United States is concentrated largely around the great lakes. The source of ore is mainly the state of Minnesota and moves by transportation over the great lakes. Canada is more fortunate than the United States in that 25 per cent of our production of basic steel is now on the Atlantic seaboard. I am all in favour of expanding in that area, as we hope to expand on the great lakes. There is no difference of opinion between us that the industry should be expanding at Sydney. I think there is room for expansion at Sydney as well as in other parts of Canada.
I do not think the hon. member seriously wants me to enter into a discussion of the Canso bridge. In the first place, I do not know much about it and I believe there is some difference of opinion among those concerned with it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I thought that was built in June, 1949?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: No, and it has not been built since. Any access is a good access in time of war, I can assure you.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Cape Breton South referred to accelerated depreciation and gave as an example the Aluminum Company of Canada. I have not the actual figures before me, but my memory is fairly good. As I remember, we allowed 60 per cent of the cost of the Shipshaw power project as accelerated depreciation, I think over four years. Then after a normal price had been set, plus all other factors that entered into it, profit, usual depreciation and so on, we allowed them to charge two and a half
916	HOUSE OF
Defence Production Act cents per pound in addition (or a large quantity of aluminum sold to the United States, I believe running to over a billion pounds, and also for aluminum sold +o the United Kingdom and I believe to Australia.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: The hon. member is quite mistaken.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: It was two and a half cents per pound in addition to the normal price of 15 cents. I am sure I am right in that respect because I went into it very carefully.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
The government of the United States made a contract with the Aluminum Company at 17J cents a pound for a certain quantity. I remember the price. I happen to know that before that quantity had been shipped, greater production allowed the Aluminum Company to lower the cost, which they did voluntarily, to 15 cents per pound.
I believe that that is the lowest price at which aluminum was ever sold in the United States.
I think the price today is either 18 or 19 cents per pound.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: The point I am making is that that was the agreement.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I think the hon. member will agree with me that the government of Canada never paid the Aluminum Company five cents for any structure or for anything except aluminum delivered to the government, and we bought very little. I might say that we got the lowest price on aluminum of anyone in the world.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I will agree with that, but by means of income tax allowances and accelerated depreciation at a time when the income tax was very high, in reality what we did was to pay for 60 per cent of the Ship-shaw development and a total of some $177 million in the way of expansion in the area. It is quite true that Canada did not put up a single dollar, but by means of various concessions the Aluminum Company was able to get 60 per cent of the Shipshaw development and the cost of other expansions.
This afternoon the minister said that perhaps they wished they had not done that at the time because of the income which has been obtained subsequently and upon which they have had to pay taxes. Let me point out to the minister that taxes came down relatively after the war. Another interesting thing is that the same suggestions for accelerated depreciation are being made today and I imagine that when the budget comes down there will be stiffer taxation than we have had in the past.
That is the point I am making and I think it is the point the hon. member was making 

a few minutes ago, although speaking from memory his figures may not have been quite right. I am sure that mine are. I quite agree with the Minister of Trade and Commerce that they did lower the price, but when you look at the cost of production in Canada and consider the large quantities they were producing you can understand why they were able to lower the price including the extra 24 cents from 174 to 15 cents per pound.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I wish my hon. friend would explain to me some time who lost money as a result of that transaction. I can assure him that it was not the government of Canada, which is now reaping taxes at the rate of some $20 million a year from that same development.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Perhaps these
specific matters could be referred to when we reach the appropriate sections. The discussion which has taken place during the last hour has covered a wide field and I am sure there are many hon. members who would like to address specific questions to the minister. I suggest that they wait until the appropriate clause is under discussion.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock the minister and some of the members on this side including myself were having a disagreement or an argument on the matter of accelerated depreciation. I did not raise the question for the purpose of holding a post mortem; I merely wanted to draw to the attention of the minister this whole question of accelerated depreciation as it applied in the last war, because I think it has very dangerous implications.
When I made a statement in reference to the Arvida and Shipshaw depreciation arrangements the minister said my figures were not correct, and I find they were not. Mine was an understatement. Of course I am conservative-minded anyway; I always want to be a bit under in order not to be caught off balance when using figures. I have the figures here; at the time I was speaking I was going by my memory. I have in my hand order in council P.C. 11745, which pretty well sets out the amounts Arvida and Shipshaw were permitted to deduct under the accelerated depreciation arrangements. I have in my other hand a copy of an agreement arising out of this order in council, between the crown and the Arvida and Shipshaw people,

which permitted! that particular operation to deduct other special depreciation allowances between 1941 and 1945. I am going to summarize the amounts paid under that order in council; they are as follows. First, regarding the expansion of aluminum production facilities at Arvida, at a cost of $117 million; depreciation allowance, June 1,	1941, to
December 31, 1945, 100 per cent as provided in P.C. 11745. That total depreciation took place in four years.
Second: contingent item of five per cent of above cost also subject to depreciation during the same period, as provided in P.C. 11745, $5,850,000.
Third: Shipshaw power development at a cost of $62,500,000; depreciation allowance, June 1, 1941, to December 31, 1945, 60 per cent as provided in P.C. 11745, $37,500,000.
Fourth: contingent item of 10 per cent of above cost also subject to 60 per cent depreciation during the same period, as provided in P.C. 11745, $3,750,000.
Regarding the expansion of aluminum producing facilities at Kingston, three items totalling $8,828,000, subject to 100 per cent special depreciation as reported by the minister at page 1487 of Hansard for March 23, 1943, $8,828,000.
Fifth: Regarding eighteen applications for special depreciation made during 1941 and 1942 totalling $4,431,956.06, subject to 100 per cent special depreciation, nine cases of 100 per cent in two years and nine cases of 100 per cent in one year, as reported in House of Commons sessional paper No. 274 of April 2, 1943, $4,431,956.06. This makes a total special depreciation allowance between 1941 and 1945 of $117,559,956.06. I might add that the total capital expenditure up to that time was $204,859,956.06. Of this total the special depreciation was more than 86 per cent, and the balance will be depreciated after 1945.
The point the minister makes is that the treasury as such did not give this money to the Aluminum Company. That is correct, but corporation taxes were waived by the government, and the taxpayers of Canada paid for the plant and equipment during that period. In my opinion if the treasury had been big-hearted and paid the bill it would not have hurt as much as the relief from taxation of corporations of that kind which were making a lot of money while at the same time we were penalizing the little fellow who just had enough to live on, making him pay his taxes while these companies amassed fortunes at the expense of the taxpayer. If the minister is looking for somebody to start a nice big plant somewhere with that kind of arrangement, I do not think it would be difficult for me and the hon. member for Winnipeg North
Defence Production Act Centre, for example, to raise the necessary capital, if the taxpayers will pay for it and let us finish up with a nice, lucrative business at the end of four or five years, with the price of the commodity we are producing sky-high. Of course the price is deliberately skyrocketed in order to write off the plant and equipment as quickly as possible, on the assumption that after the depreciation is written off the price will go down. But the price never goes down. Costs are always up, and prices stay up. As the hon. member for Melfort pointed out a few days ago, that is one of the most inflationary arrangements you could have in this country, because as that capital is depreciated it immediately becomes available for reinvestment; back goes that money into the stream of purchasing power, and away go prices.
I have in my hand sessional paper No. 274, which was a return to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre dated April 2, 1943. Now, in this sessional paper you will find order in council P.C. 421 referred to, which makes special arrangements for other aluminum producing companies in Quebec and Ontario. There are eleven in this agreement, and I am not going to put them all on the record, but I will mention this. It is the Aluminum Company of Canada Limited, Montreal and Quebec, Toronto works, a capital investment made to December 31, 1940, of $759,564.91, and it says that the above capital expenditures are to be written off in full in the year ending December 31, 1940; that is just one year. Those are just small items, and I do not want to clutter up the record by quoting from all the eleven. When you consider the depreciation allowance made to the Aluminum Company of $177,359,956.06, as set out in the figures I summarized for Arvida and the Shipshaw development, the minister I think will have to admit that the $180 million I mentioned is a conservative figure. It is really in excess of $180 million. I just wanted to clear up that point for the record, because I know the minister always tries to be, and generally is, quite accurate in his estimates to the house.
The other point I raised with him concerned his opinion as an engineer as to whether that Canso development, which the federal government has already decided upon, might not be considered as part of the defence program. I do not want him to enter into the controversy between the Department of Transport and the provincial government in Nova Scotia. At the appropriate time I intend to discuss that with the Minister of Transport for the purpose of clearing that up. Can that project be considered as part of the defence program?

Defence Production Act

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I think I should discuss the depreciation claimed by the Aluminum Company a bit more. I have never quarrelled with my hon. friend's figure of $180 million. I thought at once that it was probably more than that, as he says. I do quarrel with his statement that the money came out of the treasury of the government of Canada; that is not true by any stretch of the imagination. This is the position. The Aluminum Company of Canada had expanded immediately before the war. That pre-war expansion involved no question of accelerated depreciation. They believed they had capacity at that time to look after post-war requirements. Because of the undeveloped power they had available they were asked by the United States government to undertake an expansion which would mean multiplying their production by four or five. The United States government undertook to make that po uble by contracting for a very large amount of aluminum, and by paying for part of it in advance of production.
Now, without accelerated depreciation, what would have happened? The money was paid for aluminum, and not as capital. In that form it would have been drained off by the Canadian government. In other words, my hon. friend is quite right in saying that between the normal factors and excess profits tax that, instead of going into sticks and stones to manufacture aluminum, a large part of that money would have gone into the treasury of Canada. But the joker there is that if we had insisted on taking the money into the treasury of Canada that money would never have come to Canada because the contract would never have been made. You would never have had the power development and the aluminum plant building, because it could not have been financed without profits on that U.S. contract. The question I am asking my hon. friend to consider is this. From the viewpoint of the government of Canada, was it better to grant that accelerated depreciation and have that huge development, or would it have been better to refuse the accelerated depreciation and have nothing done whatever? That is the question, and that is the fact of the matter. There would have been no expansion.
Had the Aluminum Company foreseen the expansion in the use of the metal that has occurred in post-war years-I do not think anyone could have foreseen it-they would have desired, I imagine, to take a less accelerated depreciation. A property can only be depreciated once, and after it is fully depreciated all the earnings are then divided between the shareholders and the taxing authority. It is not regarded as good financing to take a write-off except over a long period, because depreciation then continues


to provide working capital for expansion over the longer period. My hon. friend said that they did use the wartime expansion in postwar years. They used some of it. They have never used the plant at Beauharnois since the war ended, and it represented a good many million dollars. Surely, he would say they were warranted in writing that plant off. It has been useless since then. There was a plant

I forget the location of the other plant, but it was away from Arvida- and it has never been used since the war ended. It so happens that they were able to use part of the installation at Arvida, and as the years have been passing they have been using more of it. There again I think my hon. friend will say it was a good thing for Canada that we were able to provide that accelerated depreciation to permit the plants to be built and paid for. Today we have a healthy industry that has made a tremendous contribution to the development of the Saguenay valley.
The member has made a business proposal, and I hope I shall hear more of it. He and the member for Winnipeg North Centre are going to build and pay for a plant in Winnipeg, and I am to give them special depreciation to write it off over a period. The hon. member will recall that you cannot take special depreciation except for cash paid on the line. We do not give special depreciation if the plant is built with borrowed money, or credit or anything of that sort; it must be cash actually invested in the business. If he will keep that in mind, I am sure we can get together on the proposal he has made.
As for the second question, I cannot give an opinion on the Canso situation. I have not been associated with that project. I do not even know whether the engineers have made their last report, or what the situation is. I am sure the Minister of Transport is just as anxious to get that project completed as my friend is anxious to have it completed.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, is my hon.
friend finished?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I do not intend to speak on
accelerated depreciation. In my humble view it was the premature sale of war assets. I hope in the future there will be more consideration paid to the value of everything that will be purchased or disposed of under this act.
I should like, sir, to say a word about the genealogy of this legislation. Until 1938 or 1939, the minister of national defence was the one who purchased the military supplies for his department. Then, in 1938 or 1939,

the grandfather of this act was to the effect of setting up the national defence purchasing board under the minister of finance. For the first time in our parliamentary history, the minister of finance was responsible, through that board, for the purchase of supplies for the Department of National Defence. I wonder if it was a trip given to the then minister of national defence? But his authority was emasculated and he had no power to buy a soldier's cap or uniform or anything like that. He had to send requisitions to the board for the supplies of his department. The board did not start its work at the outset because the government of the day was looking for an expert purchaser. None was found. After months of search, one of the vice-presidents of the Canadian National Railways was discovered as the one man who could head that board. During the last war we had the Department of Munitions and Supply, and I pay a tribute to the minister for the excellent work he did to stimulate Canadian businessmen to produce for the various departments he was supplying.
There is one thing I want to tell the minister, and I am sorry to have to repeat it; it is about the application of this bill. The minister is a member of the government whom I support; he has my confidence. Otherwise I would declare myself against his legislation. I am ready to give him a free hand to the limit. But what is the limit? Everything under this act is done under his own supervision, as much as it can physically be done, and under his control. Now we come to the control of expenditures. I am not in a position to discuss all the ramifications of the aluminum trust; it is not my intention to do so. But we have before us a piece of legislation that will give tremendous powers to a member of the government, and at the same time he will be given the exercise of that power probably in virtue of the emergency legislation. These two acts will be Siamese twins. The government will have to do that precisely for the purpose of putting in force the legislation that we have before us. It is something tremendous. If that legislation is submitted to us now, it is for the reason that in any case of emergency, when parliament is not sitting, the government will have to take advantage of both acts to do certain things that will be required in the public interest. That is clear and evident. It is precisely for that reason that the Prime Minister has said that, as soon as we meet together, he will table the orders in council if they are passed during the recess or during the adjournment.
This is a new department. The minor civil servants will be appointed by the civil service
Defence Production Act commission; but the big fellows will be technicians, and they will be appointed by order in council. I remember quite distinctly that when the Defence Purchases Act was passed twelve or thirteen years ago, a member of the opposition asked the government how the appointments would be made. The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), who was then a member of the government, said with great candour that assuredly they would all be made by the civil service commission. Everybody laughed and the matter ended there. But few people except minor civil servants were appointed by the civil service commission. I have no objection to the appointment by the minister himself of everybody in the department, upon one condition, namely, that we can know, upon request, the salary of each member of a crown company.
I refer not only to high officials; I refer to high officials, major officials, and minor officials. I include everybody. Why? Because it is the duty of members of parliament to give that information to any of their constituents who request it.
During the war and after the war I waged a fight for the reform of public accounts precisely in order to protect the government against abuse. I want to be proud of the government that I support. If I tell them that, it is not at all because I am opposed to them. It is because I am a supporter of the government. I consider myself to be a good Liberal, although I am not always called orthodox. But it is the doctrine that I have known, as enunciated by those who have been the stalwarts of the party up until the present Prime Minister took charge as its leader.
Let me give an example of what I mean. For instance, in one of those crown companies, if a gentleman is appointed by order in council, he considers himself to be superior to those who have been appointed by the civil service commission. He is a gentleman by virtue of his own rank, by order in council. He may owe something to the government but he owes nothing to parliament, and he has a supreme contempt for members of parliament because their indemnity is less than the salaries that are paid to these gentlemen. Our travelling expenses are also less. Therefore it is thought we must be less competent than those gentlemen.
I am serious when I say that. I do not want to hinder the success of the operation of this legislation; but in my humble view, what will best serve the minister is respect for our parliamentary institution on the part of all those who now belong to the crown companies or who will be appointed hereafter in this large department. Members of parliament-I can say this of all members of

Defence Production Act parliament, but especially of the supporters of the government-are the shock-absorbers of the government.
If the members of the opposition do not have to defend government policy, they must be in a position to explain it to any one of their constituents. What I am saying now is British parliamentary doctrine that I have read in big books, the names of which I have forgotten. But I remember the main idea of those who have written these textbooks, which are based on the soundest rulings of the British Speakers. Therefore, sir, there should be no different classes of public servants. We should all serve the people. We may support the government; we cannot serve the government. The gentlemen who belong to the crown companies are not servants of the government. They are, as we are ourselves, servants of the great country that is Canada. It must be said of each one of them, and it must be said of the big and the small ones.
My conclusion is clear. The minister does not agree with it. In my heart I am convinced that he is wrong about it. My warning is not unfriendly to all those big gentlemen who come here and consider that the position of controllers, and so forth, constitute a kind of nobility. I know a gentleman who is a personal friend of the minister, as he is a friend of mine. He was controller of light. His duty consisted in deciding what we had to do about daylight saving. Well, any child could have been light controller and could have said that in the summer we must have more hours of sunlight than in the winter. But he was a controller, and it was something much more than O.B.E., C.B.E. and M.B.E.; it was something real.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Was the hon. member able to find out his salary?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: No; I think it was one dollar.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: How much were his expenses?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
What I say tonight is not very pleasant for me to say, but if I say it it is because I believe it. My record is in Hansard about the necessity of inspiring and of teaching to all the fundamental principle of the government of our country. Wherever I have the honour to speak outside the house I never fail to tell the people that I consider myself their servant. Why should anyone think differently? What is right does not need to be concealed. What is right can be exposed and defended in public meetings anywhere, and no one should be afraid to do so.
Now, sir, there is another point that I wish to make before I take my seat. It is this one.


There are many false interpretations of the duties held by some people in major positions outside the civil service. It is that they would be humiliated to have their remuneration, their salary, their living and travelling expenses, appear in the public accounts. Why? When they receive a cheque they cash it at the bank. It passes through many hands, and I wonder why there is not such a check upon the duties of all those gentlemen. I shall try to mention this just as objectively as possible, just as one writes a thesis to get a degree.
Very often members of parliament receive no reply from those crown companies unless they write to the minister. Why is it that it is impossible to get some information from those concerns about matters of great importance to our constituents? I will quote no particular incident, but I wish to congratulate the minister on having appointed to the Canadian Commercial Corporation a gentleman from Quebec city who answers the letters that we send to him. It is an immense improvement.
I will say nothing about the gentleman who is the head of Canadian Arsenals Limited, Brigadier Theriault of Quebec, who is a most helpful and well qualified man. He answers letters, too. There are many others who have a strong contempt for members of parliament. They say it is mixing into politics when they answer letters sent to them by a member of parliament.
I want the minister to be just as free as possible in his important duties. I do not want him to be handicapped by undue correspondence from me or from any one of my colleagues, but when I write to anyone in any of these crown companies as a member of parliament I am entitled to an answer and to the right answer. If these gentlemen consider that it is outside their duties tc answer my letter as it should be, the thing they have to do is to tell me to get in touch with the minister, and then I will have a good excuse to write to him, the excuse that one of his officials has suggested to me tc write to him.
What I have said does not apply to the deputy minister of trade and commerce for the very good reason that his salary and his expenses appear in the public accounts just the same as the salary and travelling expenses of some other officials appear there; but I repeat, the best protection of the government against any abuse-I do not mention embezzlement or misuse of funds; I speak of abuse of authority-is the respect of our parliamentary institution and of the members of parliament by all those who are in the pay

of the dominion government, whether it is one dollar a year or $35,000 a year, plus expenses.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. member
why he objects to the route of obtaining information through the minister's office? That is a carefully prepared route. We try to see that the information given out is accurate, and we try to see that it is given promptly. I would be sorry to dispose of that route for obtaining information, because I think it is pretty good.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I will tell the minister that I am thankful for his answer. I have no objection at all to writing to him. But what I am telling him again is that it is physically impossible for him to answer all requests from members of parliament. It is because I want to give him as free a hand as possible in the fulfilment of his numerous and onerous duties that I want to write to him the least possible number of times, asking him for information. But when he has decided something is to be done somewhere, it seems to me members of parliament should be entitled to an answer.
There could be abuse from some members who might ask indiscreet questions. But then the staff of the crown company could easily answer, "It is up to the minister to decide whether you are entitled to that information or not."
Now, I turn to another matter.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

I am speaking for myself; I have no power to speak on behalf of the government. However, I am sincere in what I do, and that gives me the right to answer the hon. member. If my hon. friend continues to insist upon such picayune matters, if he insists upon asking questions about patronage in connection with crown companies, and all that sort of thing, it would destroy my argument and it would mean that members of the House of Commons do not ask serious questions, or questions requiring replies.
I have discussed the matter objectively without any thought of political partisanship. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre takes the opposite stand. He always thinks that by speaking as he does in the house he will gain more votes for the C.C.F.; and that is his great mistake.

On section 2-Definitions.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I should like to ask a question about the definition of the expression "associated government". I see that in the definition it includes any nation of the British commonwealth of nations, and also any nation which is a member of the North Atlantic treaty organization. Then it goes on to include also the government of any other country designated by order in council as being a country the defence of which is vital to the defence of Canada.
How would that be treated? This would seem to be a serious decision to be made by order in council. How would it be handled, so far as parliament is concerned?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I do not wish to give an answer which would be indicative of anything
922	HOUSE OF
Defence Production Act that is under contemplation. However, there are in the North Atlantic treaty a group of twelve nations. The one in the Mediterranean farthest eastward is Italy. There might be something occurring in Greece that the twelve nations of the North Atlantic treaty would consider was a menace to their own security. If that took place they would be regarded as an associated government in any active resistance that was being sponsored by themselves and the nations of the North Atlantic treaty. I am just giving that as one example. It was to cover things of that kind that this extension was made to the original definition, which was limited to the commonwealth countries and the North Atlantic treaty countries.
However, it was felt that there might occur a situation where it would be regarded as being in the interests of either the commonwealth countries or the group in the North Atlantic treaty to treat some government that was not actually a party in either group as pursuing a common purpose with the rest of us.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Sometimes I am a little uncertain as to whether, when we refer to the commonwealth of nations, we include only the self-governing dominions. Would this include crown colonies?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: We have no direct relations with crown colonies. The relations of Canada are with the United Kingdom, and anything that concerns a crown colony is handled through United Kingdom channels.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I should like to ask a question concerning section 2(k) which states:
"Mark-up" means the amount added to cost in determining the selling price to cover overhead and profit.
A while ago we were talking about accelerated depreciation. If the government enters into a contract with a firm to extend its plant to produce something the government wants, and allows accelerated depreciation, it does not mean a thing to the company unless the mark-up on the price is sufficient to allow the company to take that accelerated depreciation. A company has to make a profit before it can obtain accelerated depreciation to write off the cost of its plant. What method have the government of determining whether that plant has been built economically? The government is the only buyer of the product being made. What method have the government of determining whether the plant is being operated efficiently? It seems to me that there must be great difficulty in determining what is the fair price and1 what is a fair margin to allow, and also what is a reasonable profit which should be made so that they may claim a mark-up.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Mark-up applies more particularly to retail sales, where a firm buys a product and resells it to the public. I can think of no situation where accelerated depreciation would be allowed to a retailer. Where a plant is being built to turn out a product for sale to the government it is not a matter of mark-up, it is a matter of cost of production. Accelerated depreciation would not enter into the cost of production. The proprietor of a plant may have other portions of the plant that are earning a profit and he can apply the accelerated depreciation against his other earnings. He could show a loss on his business and apply the money lost to accelerated depreciation if he thought it was wise to do so.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Assume that I am a manufacturer of farm machinery. I have trained personnel and have the technique to produce, say, a gun barrel. The government wants me to produce that article and will allow me accelerated depreciation to pay the cost of an additional plant and to be spread over a period of four years, as was done in the last war. How do you determine whether that plant is being constructed economically? How do you determine whether you are paying a fair price for the product which only takes care of the accelerated depreciation, which in turn allows only normal profits?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
As far as construction goes, we have a large and widespread construction organization whose business it is to check the costs of construction and to see that it is carried out in an economical way. If the inspection staff reports that it believes the contract is not being well carried out, steps are taken to investigate the situation and appropriate action would follow.
Take the case of a firm making agricultural implements that is asked to make guns. How would we know what is a reasonable price for guns? The treasury cost accountants go into the plant and determine the cost of labour and the cost of material. The profit is fixed in the contract and adding together all elements of cost the price is determined accordingly. That is why we have the power of renegotiation. The cost of the guns would vary from time to time, and generally the cost is lower as time goes on.
The hon. member asks where the money would come from with which to write off the accelerated depreciation of the new plant. It probably would come from the earnings of the old plant. That is where it usually comes from. In other words, this manufacturer could take his earnings from the agricultural implement business to depreciate the new plant.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
In paragraph (i) of section 2 it is stated:
(i) "government issue" means machinery, machine tools, equipment or defence supplies furnished by the minister-
Does that mean that a committee will set up priorities on machine tools as was done during the war?

speechtext: We have a machine tool controller, but in some cases the government buys machine tools or a certain part of a finished product and supplies it to the contractor as a free issue. That definition refers to furnished products of that kind.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: And machine tools?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Sometimes.

speechtext: Before the hon. member for Temiscouata leaves the chamber I should like to speak to this section as I think he may have something to say about it as well. I disagree thoroughly with the position taken by the hon. member for Temiscouata with respect to patronage.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
But I agree with the hon. member as to the importance of retaining the practice of using the civil service commission as far as it possibly can be done, even in a department such as this. I notice that section 4 provides that such officers, clerks and employees as are necessary for the proper conduct of the business of the department may be appointed in the manner authorized by law. That means they are to be appointed by the civil service commission.

The provision in the act passed last fall obviously was not meant to give the minister power to turn over this wide discretionary authority to anyone he saw fit. It reads:
The minister may authorize persons to act under his control and direction on his behalf in the exercise of powers conferred on him by this act or regulation.
The sidenote is, "Minister empowered to authorize persons to act under his control." The obvious interpretation of that provision of the statute passed last year is that the discretion would be exercised by the minister; that whoever was acting for him would merely carry out the acts he authorized. Under section 5 of the present bill, however, the minister can turn over his discretionary power not only to his deputy or to an associate deputy, but to anyone he sees fit. For example an order may be issued to take over a man's business; power is taken under this act to appoint someone to do that. Under section 5 of this bill a drastic order of that kind could be made by anyone appointed by the minister. The discretion can be exercised by someone other than the minister, someone in no way responsible to parliament, upon whom we would have no check whatever.
I do suggest that the powers given the minister under this bill are such that they should be exercised by him, and that section 5 is not necessary. It is not sound legislation; it is unfair to the individual Canadian, and also unfair to parliament. We would ask that the clause be deleted.
