speechtext: Will the companies that may be in existence now and those which may be set up in the future be brought under the provisions of this bill? Will they be paid for materials sold by them, and will the money be kept in the corporation's hands, or will it be turned into the revolving fund which is set up by a later section of this bill?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
The revolving fund neither increases nor decreases. It is simply what the names implies, a fund out of which money is paid but with that money to be recovered at a later stage and returned to the fund.
If one of the crown companies sells a product for war purposes it will sell in the normal way and be paid for it in the normal way. In other words, it is just another contractor as far as the government is concerned.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: The crown company is just another contractor?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: That is all.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I understand the minister to say that the moneys received by a crown company from sales of its products under a defence contract will not go into the revolving fund, but remain assets of the company and be returned to that company.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: That is correct.

Section agreed to.
Section 8 agreed to.
On section 9-Administration of department under the minister.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: What is the significance of the word "exclusively" in line one of the second paragraph of clause 9? Does that indicate that the power of delegation which we have been talking about a little earlier does not apply here at all?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: That was to indicate that this would be the sole agency for the government to do the things that the department or the minister, as the head of the department, is empowered by the act to do, and there would be no other procurement agencies for the objects covered by this bill.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: As a matter of explanation, why is the word "minister" used instead of the department, because the department is actually the agency of government set up for the purpose of doing these things. Why is it not proper that it should be "the department, exclusively, may buy or otherwise acquire", because in the cases where the minister is empowered to act on behalf of the department I should think that would apply, and also it would appear then clearly that it is the agency of the government that exclusively is going to do this; whereas the word "exclusively" related to the word minister might appear to give a different meaning.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
In all the departments it is the minister who is given the powers to act. That is the form in which all the departments are set up. There is the Department 80709-59
Defence Production Act of Justice, but the powers to be exercised by the minister. We do however recognize some distinctions. Sometimes the minister of one department is put in charge of something that is not within his department. Thus, the Minister of Justice is the minister responsible for the administration of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. That is not a part of the functions of the department; but the functions of the department are in these various statutes stated to be the powers and duty and responsibility of the minister.
I do not know that I would have drafted that section just in that way, "the minister exclusively", but that is the way in which it appeared in the munitions and supply act and in the Defence Supplies Act. The Defence Supplies Act, section 4, states:
The minister, exclusively, may buy or otherwise acquire defence supplies and construct or carry out projects required by the Department of National Defence, except
(a)	projects to be constructed or carried out by persons in the employ of His Majesty in right of Canada; and
(b)	such defence supplies or projects as the minister may, with the concurrence of the Minister of National Defence, request the Department of National Defence to procure, construct or carry out, as the case may be.
It is the form that has been usual.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I was relating my remarks to the explanation given by the Prime Minister. As I understood what the Prime Minister said, it was to the effect that it was intended by this subsection of section 9 to make it clear that this would be the only agency for the purchase of defence supplies. If that is so, then it would seem to me that this was different from the use of the word "exclusively" as applied to the minister in the other acts, where it seemed that the use of the word "exclusively" there was really for the purpose of showing that the minister exclusively within that department would have authority to make these purchases.
I was under the impression from what the Prime Minister said that in this case it was intended to convey the understanding that only this department, and the minister of this department, would be buying defence supplies. It was for that reason that it seemed to me that the word "department" would be more suitable-or a combination of both.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
It has been in this form. We possibly will not complete the whole bill tonight. This can be brought to the attention of the officers of the Department of Justice, as to whether or not it would be more workable with the word "department" added or substituted. But it is the way in which it
930	HOUSE OF
Defence Production Act was expressed in the Department of Munitions and Supply Act, and the way it was expressed in the Defence Supplies Act. However, we will ask them if there would be any improvement in the substitution.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I wish to make it clear that I
am not in this instance opposing it. I am simply seeking to avoid misunderstanding as to the use of the word, having regard to the explanation that has been given. I put it forward as a suggestion, that there is a possibility that in the other acts there was a different method, in view of the fact that there were certain defence purchases being made in other departments at that time.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I should like to raise another question in connection with section 9. I would point out that in subsection 2 (b) the expression "Department of National Defence" is used rather than the expression "the minister." It refers to such defence supplies, and so on, as the minister may "request the Department of National Defence to procure or construct."
What is contemplated in paragraph (b)? It seems to me that over the past year, and particularly during the two sessions of last year, the process was to divest the Minister of National Defence of the responsibility and the administrative concern in connection with purchases for his department, and to place them more and more under the Canadian Commercial Corporation, and now under the defence production department. Yet it seems here there is something contemplated which would reserve or hand back to the Department of National Defence the responsibility for making purchases. Would the minister explain what is meant there?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
That paragraph is to permit
provision for local purchases. For example we may get a letter from the Minister of National Defence addressed to me stating that it would be helpful if those concerned at a project at Suffield had the privilege of buying fresh vegetables, and asking if an allowance of $500 a month could be made for that purpose. I would write the Minister of National Defence asking him to arrange for the purchase of vegetables at Suffield to the extent of $500 a month. It simply gives permission.
Section 9 stands.
Sections 10 to 13 inclusive agreed to.
On section 14-Stockpiling.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Would the minister tell us the relationship between this section and section 30? I notice that section 14 refers to such materials or substances as may be designated


by the governor in council as materials or substances essential to the needs of the community of which it is advisable to maintain stock to safeguard against possible shortages thereof. When one puts that section beside section 30, which refers to essential materials and services, and defines them as those essential to meet the requirements of the defence forces of Canada, 1 think there emerges a significant difference between sections 14 and 30. It seems to me section 14 goes considerably outside the scope of mere defence production or defence purchasing. It is at least giving a very much enlarged interpretation to the word "defence" and it seems to me it raises possibilities which require some explanation.
It is the intention through section 14 to enable the minister, if material is in short supply, whether it is immediately related to defence and the immediate needs of our defence forces or not, to purchase it, and to exercise all the powers he is given under this act with respect to that material?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: No; the purpose of the section is to provide for the stockpiling of materials not readily available, should certain contingencies develop. For instance, it would refer to tin, which would be in short supply if Malaya fell, or to antimony, which is in short supply, or to quartz crystals, which come from certain areas that are trouble spots, and where supplies might be interrupted at critical times. This is the section which gives the minister power to acquire, store, maintain, transport and sell materials of that type.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: For the community?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Yes, for the community.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I wonder why it is necessary to have section 14. "Essential material" is defined as a material or substance designated by the governor in council under section 30 as an essential material.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: That is an essential material under the act which allows the control of essential materials. But there is nothing in that section which allows the government to buy and sell strategic materials. That is the point in section 14-it authorizes the government to buy and resell.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: That contemplates buying and reselling to our allies?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: It might be to the general public. It is to provide stockpiles of scarce materials or materials which may become otherwise unobtainable in the event of war in certain areas.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
As a matter of interest-and I think it is important-I wonder why that is

put in defence production, and why it would not normally come under the minister's functions as Minister of Trade and Commerce?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: As my hon. friend will see, it comes under the general heading of "organization of industry for defence".

Section agreed to.
On section 15-Ministerial powers to acquire and dispose of supplies.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: How is section 15 (f) to be carried out? I see that under section 16 loans are excluded, and such loans cannot be made from the revolving fund. Thus section 15 does not contain the expression "if authorized by parliament the minister may", and so on. Since the minister cannot make such loans by way of the revolving fund under section 16, from where will the money come to make the loans contemplated in section 15 (f)?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Money is appropriated by parliament for that purpose. Certain moneys have been appropriated under the national defence vote. If it is necessary to give capital assistance to a project it can be given only by obtaining money from the Department of National Defence. For example, we found it necessary to finance the Orenda plant in Toronto. That money was sent over as an encumbrance on the vote of the Department of National Defence. In the estimates for next year there may be a vote for capital purposes under the defence production department but, if so, it will be placed before parliament and voted on in the usual way.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Perhaps I should ask this question of the Prime Minister. Is it usual when such advances are to be authorized that they can be made only if an appropriation is passed by parliament? Is it not usual to preface these paragraphs with the words, the minister, when authorized by parliament, may" so there win be no question that it cannot be done out of the revolving fund or by general authority?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
To have the words, "the minister, when authorized by parliament" would mean that each individual advance would have to be authorized by parliament. If parliament sees fit to make a sum available it will not be part of the revolving fund that is to be provided by this bill. It is something that will have to be brought up each year in the form of a special vote in the estimates. If there is no vote appearing in the estimates, loans cannot be made. As has been discussed already, there was some $50 million provided for advances on defence production. The application of parts of that $50 million could be made under this, but unless there is a fund
80709-59J
Defence Production Act provided, capital assistance cannot be taken out of the revolving fund that this bill contemplates.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
The Prime Minister says,
"unless there is an item in the estimates." These expenditures would not come before parliament and parliament would not have a chance to vote on them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: If in this bill a certain amount was being asked for for capital advances there would be no requirement for an estimate. We do not think that there should be anything asked for at this time beyond the revolving fund. We think that the revolving fund provided for in the next section can be satisfactorily explained. It is to be a revolving fund merely for temporary and provisional use, to be reimbursed by the department or the associated government or whoever it is that gets the finished product. As we had no specific capital advance in contemplation that we could bring to parliament we did not think it was proper to ask for any in this bill. We think we should have to bring in that estimate and possibly say to parliament what the plans are and why the estimate is being requested.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: If that is the case, why is it necessary to include this power in the bill before us?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: We are setting out here what will be the powers of the minister. Of course we enjoy these discussions, but we would rather have no more of them than are required. We are asking for the powers with which the minister may be clothed in order to carry out such things as are apt to be required. But the powers will not be exercised unless parliament provides some department with funds that can be used as capital advances. If parliament provides the Department of National Defence with funds that may be used as capital advances, they will have to be handled by the Minister of National Defence.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
The Minister of National
Defence has been given authority to make commitments, I think up to about $500 million, in future years. Could that authority be used to cover advances under this section 15?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
If there was a loan to be made it could not be made under the commitments. There can be tooling up or tools purchased by the Department of National Defence out of funds provided to that department in order to facilitate the production of certain things required by the department. In connection with the Orenda engine there

Defence Production Act have been acquired by the Department of National Defence tools which are used in the plant to produce the engines.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: That would be regarded as a capital advance?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: That would be regarded, not as a loan but as an advance payment on engines to be delivered to the department.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: You say that that would come out of the estimate or appropriation under the estimates?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: There have been earmarked out of the commitments certain sums that will be part of the purchase price of the Orenda engine.

Section agreed to.
On section 16-Defence production revolving fund.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I want to make a comment, ask a question and inquire as to the possibility of having some change made in section 16. I hope the fact that sections such as 15, 11 and others have been passed with almost no comment on our part is a clear indication that we meant what we said when we indicated that we wanted to give generous powers and to make this act workable. I understand that what will happen under the operation of the revolving fund will be that a working capital of $100 million will be set up, and then there will be incomings and outgoings for various purposes which I shall not read and detail at the moment. I want to be sure that my understanding is correct that parliament will really have no knowledge of the operations which take place until eventually they are recorded in the public accounts. If I am correct in that, then I go on to-

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I told the hon, member for Vancouver-Quadra that I would be glad to insert a section providing for an annual report of the department. Such annual report would certainly give the position of the revolving fund. If the department enters into a contract on behalf of the Department of National Defence or with any foreign government then by means of this revolving fund it can finance the contract temporarily, pay the contractors promptly and make demand on the Department of National Defence when there is a finished product to offer. If it conducts its affairs prudently, as we try to do, there should be no loss to the department. It is simply a temporary accommodation. It would be quite illegal or improper to use it for any permanent commitment of any kind. For instance, we could not use it for capital investment purposes.

It must be money that will come back into the fund with reasonable promptness, not later than the completion of the asset which is being built.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
The minister's agreement to make an annual report certainly would be an improvement. Nevertheless, as I tried to suggest the other evening, it seems to me there is a whole world of difference between what went on during the war and what goes on now. That is so for this very simple reason, as I see it, that the minister is now organizing the functions of his department to complete the three year defence plan which was outlined by the Minister of National Defence. I cannot understand why it is not possible for the minister of the new department to come to this house with his estimates for the year. There would have to be a good deal of leeway, I should think; probably there would have to be quite a large amount of working capital, and perhaps this $100 million is not too much. But I am suggesting that along with that I see no reason why the minister could not come to this house in very large measure exactly as the Minister of National Defence does and say "I have certain expenditures to make this year, and I have certain commitments."
Let me give an illustration which I ventured to give the other evening. Let us take the matter of uniforms. A certain number of uniforms will be required next year by the Department of National Defence, and I should imagine the number would be known pretty accurately now. If that is so the minister of defence production will have to supply the raw materials; I understand that would be part of the functions of this department. I am quite unable to understand why that item could not be brought in here and approved as an estimate of this department, just as the national defence estimates are brought in. Let me say again that I have not, nor has anyone else in this party, any intention of chiselling, of trying to hold the minister down to such a point as to make his task impossible, or even difficult. Would it not be reasonable to ask the minister to bring in his estimates as far as that may be humanly possible?
Another point I want to raise is whether there is any reason why contracts, as they are made, should not be laid on the table of this house? I will come to the question of security in a moment. That question was raised this afternoon by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. My suggestion, supported by what I have observed in connection with the Minister of National Defence and other ministers of the government, is that in this country where things are done as publicly as they are, we are just fooling ourselves if we imagine they are not known by

our potential enemies. Therefore to say we are giving away anything by bringing an estimate into this house is just contrary to what we believe to be the facts.
Let me put this to the minister and to the Prime Minister as something I hope can be done. Some of us feel very earnestly that the rights of parliament are perhaps too lightly dealt with at times. On the other hand I believe we have shown that we have a practical approach to this matter, and that we want to enable the minister of defence production to carry out his important function.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: If I may answer the last question first, I think the number of contracts for defence supplies placed last year runs to about 80,000. There is no objection to putting the 80,000 on the table, but my hon. friends knows he can get any contract placed by the department of defence production by simply asking for it on the order paper and having it made a return.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I intended to specify contracts above a certain amount. We would not want to make the thing ridiculous, of course.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Unless the limit was pretty high you would still have a tremendous number of contracts laid on the table. If my hon. friend has a reasonable request and puts it on the order paper, it will be considered; he will be told the amount of work involved, and if he still wants it he will get it. There is no desire whatever to hold back information from the house as far as contracts are concerned. As to the proposal that instead of a revolving fund the department of defence production should have a vote to cover these expenditures-

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
As far as
possible. I did not exclude some part of a revolving fund.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: We will assume you mean to have a vote.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
And a commitment, like
national defence.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
That would mean a complete duplication of the estimates. Without specific authorization there is no way you can revolve money in a government account. In other words money received in a department does not go to that department; it goes to the Receiver General of Canada. The money is paid from the funds voted by parliament. In other words there are two separate accounts, one for receipts and the other for expenditures, and you are never allowed to transfer funds from one to the other. It means a good deal of padding of the estimates in any event; but to use that kind of
Defence Production Act accounting for what we require in the department of defence production would pretty well mean that we would have to get money voted to the Department of National Defence and also have money voted to the department of defence production in order to carry out the projects, or else continue to follow the plan we have been following and require a complete transfer of the full cost of a project before we can commence to carry it out. We are trying to get away from the latter. It is simply a matter of mechanics, and we have to get legislation because without it the process is quite unworkable.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I am afraid I have not made myself clear, and I do not think the minister has completely understood me. I quite recognize that the minister will require a certain amount of working capital, that there will have to be something in the nature of a revolving fund covering part of his activities. That will be necessary, for instance, under section 16 (a), to pay the cost of acquisition, maintenance, transportation of stocks of materials, and so on. Later on it provides that these may be sold. So I realize that there must be working capital and a certain leeway in that respect. On the other hand I do suggest that a very considerable portion of what the minister is going to spend will be for materials the need for which is known in advance. Indeed, it seems to me that comes directly within what the Prime Minister was describing a few minutes ago in connection with the estimate covering the Orenda engines. All we are endeavouring to do, without interfering with the undertakings the emergency demands, is to preserve as far as possible the right of parliament to scrutinize expenditures. I think the minister will agree that if section 16 is carried as is, parliament will have no control of any kind over the expenditures that are made, except in authorizing the original $100 million, and except in cases where losses are incurred, when the legislation says they must come back to parliament.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will permit me to interject for a moment, he will have exactly the same control over expenditures that he has without the revolving fund. That fund is simply a mechanism. It is not the minister of defence production who buys and pays for these articles. He buys them temporarily, but he acts as agent for the Department of National Defence. That department has an appropriation to cover any purchases, and in the end they pay for them. In the meantime, rather than get the money from them in advance to pay our contractors, we will have this revolving fund available to
934	HOUSE OF
Defence Production Act cover interim payments. Through its use we can deliver the finished article to the defence department at the time we exact payment for it. The revolving fund has no significance as far as spending public money is concerned. In the last war we had a bulk appropriation for all war purposes. We would get an appropriation of perhaps $300 or $400 million. The revolving fund came out of that appropriation, that is a certain amount of it was used as a revolving fund. It did not represent expenditures, but simply meant the temporary use of money. We did it under the War Measures Act. We made provision so that the money could be used as a revolving fund, and eventually charged to the recipient of the goods. That is all we are asking now- that the revolving fund be spelled out and an amount fixed by parliament to be used for that purpose.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Surely it is true, notwithstanding what the minister has said-he has described the way the fund is used and the way the defence department will eventually get an appropriation and repay the fund; items will go in and out. What I am still asking and pointing out to the minister is that all that goes on without any knowledge or control by parliament. I am still asking whether in respect of a great deal of that it cannot be done in the estimates. Could it not be done in the manner that the estimates for the Department of National Defence are handled at the present time? I believe it can. Will the minister be good enough to take a look at it in that sense and let this section stand?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Surely my hon. friend can understand that the department of defence production does not buy anything for itself. It simply acts as an agent.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
It may buy
with your permission.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
It may buy stationery or something like that, but ordinarily it buys for someone else. It does not get an appropriation from parliament to buy things; that is done by other departments. The defence department gets an appropriation to buy things through the agency of the defence production department.
A foreign government may request something and make arrangements with parliament to pay for it.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: What about stockpiling?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: We would get an appropriation for stockpiling.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
The minister
says his department does not buy things, so there is no point in bringing in estimates. Let [Mr. Howe.)

us take the illustration I gave, and there must be a hundred like it, the question of material for uniforms. Is there any reason why you should not come to parliament this year and say that you want so many millions of dollars to buy textiles for uniforms? Is there any reason why that should not happen? If it can happen in that case, is there any reason why it should not happen in a great many others?

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: As I said before, we could do that. We could get an appropriation from parliament to buy cloth, and then in the usual course of events the cloth would be made into uniforms which would be delivered to the Department of National Defence. The full cost of the uniforms would be returned to the department of defence production, and then you have a double entry-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Then you have voted the money twice.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: That is the only way it can be done without the revolving fund. You are then in the position of voting the money twice.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Surely, the minister is elevating the thing-

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I am not, and if my hon. friend will think it over and come back and say he has got someone to explain it to him, I am prepared to let the clause stand. It is so clear to everyone else in the house. I hope he will not insist on standing it over.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I am sorry
the minister is so troubled by my stupidity, but I am really unrepentant. I am not impressed by the bookkeeping difficulties, and I am quite sure the minister is not either. You can always make books agree with common sense.

speechtext:
This section contains some pretty wide powers of appointment of controllers to take over the business of a person who the minister is satisfied has failed, or is likely to fail, to perform the contract efficiently and in a businesslike manner, or when a person who has been directed to enter into a defence contract is likely to fail to perform it to the satisfaction of the minister. Therefore you have a double element of compulsion: firstly, the person can be directed to take the contract, even though we have not a war, according to the definition; and secondly, having been directed to take it, the minister can then say: I do not think you are going to perform it efficiently, and I therefore appoint a controller to take over your business. That controller can take over, according to the clause as it stands, not only that part of the business which relates to or is necessarily a part of the defence contract, but the whole of the business. There is no limitation on the power at all.
It seems to me that the power is unnecessarily wide. I should think that the minister might be willing to accept some limitation upon the power, not to bind the controllers, but on the powers which these controllers may exercise; because, Mr. Chairman, if you


look at the last words of paragraph (c) of subsection 1 of section 27 you will see that:
The minister may authorize another person (in this act called a "controller") to carry on, until the minister otherwise directs, the whole or any part of the business of that person.
Then, if you look at subsection 2 you will see that the controller can be directed by the minister to:
Do all such things as he thinks fit for the purpose of carrying on the business or that part thereof.
In other words, he can be directed to do anything with respect to the whole of the business, even though only part of the business is related to or necessarily involved in the defence contract.
Again, in clause 2 there is no limitation upon the time within which the controller shall maintain control and direction of the business, so that it may be extended. There is nothing here to indicate that the power to control, and the control of the business, will terminate when the contract is performed or the direction is complied with.
While I am not going to make an argument at the moment as to whether or not that tremendous power should be given, I should like to ask the minister or the Prime Minister whether he does not think that it would be acceptable to place there a limitation which would specifically restrict the powers of the controller to that part of the business necessarily concerned with the defence contract or the direction; and secondly, to limit the power of the controller to such time as the defence contract may be performed or the direction may be in existence, so that when the contract is fulfilled it automatically would follow that the controller is no longer in power over that business? You would not then cut down what is desired, as I understand it, namely, the power to get the contract performed. It would mean that you could not go any further than that, and could not control the business after the contract had been performed.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
No. I think any restriction would tend to defeat the objective of the clause. In the last war we had a good many contractors, some strong and some weak. They got into trouble one way or another. Perhaps they were not keeping their books properly. Perhaps they were diverting the money from one operation to another, or perhaps they were just incompetent and were rapidly going bankrupt. We had cases of that kind. We put a controller in on a good many of them. Ordinarily you cannot separate the business into one part one thing and another part another. Usually, if it is under the same

roof it is interrelated. I do not know of any cases where we put a controller in that he did not take charge certainly of all operations under one roof. He stays there. It may take a long time. I had one controller in one plant for three years, until he got the plant out of insolvency and back into operation efficiently where it was able to settle its accounts with the government.
The government is responsible for the acts of any controller it appoints. If any man thinks a controller makes things worse instead of better he can take the government into court. I think there is ample protection for the public. We have not had any complaint. I know of no case where a controller has not straightened out a bad situation and left it much better than he found it.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I am not objecting to the right to appoint a controller, or to instruct or require that controller to straighten out the business, to use the minister's own terms, for the performance of the defence contract. But I find here, I repeat, no limitation on the extent to which he can take possession of the business. It may not necessarily be a big business in the sense of big industry. It may be a business engaged in two or three separate activities under the one company or the one individual; and yet the clause here gives power to appoint a controller to take over the whole of the business, even though the other parts are not in any way concerned with or related to the defence contract, or direction, about which the minister is concerned. If the minister will consider the thing I am sure he will agree that there is a possibility of limitation on the power there to make it clear that the appointment relates only to that part of the business concerned with the war contract or the direction.

speechtext:
There is one feature in this that it seems to me should be borne in mind, and it has to do with the general observations that were made about this measure earlier. The remark was made by the hon. member

Defence Production Act for Vancouver-Quadra that the whole approach seemed to be different from that in connection with other considerations that were before the house.
I do not believe that those are unrelated. What seems to be so obvious is the disproportion between the extent of the measures called for here and the attitude of the government in regard to other matters connected with defence which are certainly of equal importance. If it is so necessary to take that sweeping power in connection with production, then it seems to me strangely disproportionate and unreal to have so little regard for the state of our defence forces.
The attitude toward the defence forces is that we are in a position where we can go forward under reasonably normal conditions in that respect. Here we have before us powers so wide and so sweeping that, as the minister has said, there is really no difference between what we are asked for here and what we would have in an all-out shooting war.
Let us see how far this goes. It is not only that the minister may decide that he thinks someone is going to fail-which is a very sweeping power at a time when we are told we should still seek to impress upon the minds of the public that we are not really in a state which approximates an all-out struggle -but it goes further. I would call this particularly to the attention of the Prime Minister.
In section 27(2) there is provision that where a controller has been appointed to carry on a business or a part thereof he shall be deemed to be the agent of the owner thereof for the purpose of carrying on the business. Now, let us see exactly how far that goes. He is not merely the representative of the government; he is the agent of the owner. As the agent of the owner he is in a position to impose upon the owner all the legal consequences of that agency, whether it is to the benefit of the owner or not. This goes much further than merely saying that the controller may go in and carry on the business.
It does not seem to me that we should go so far in the first place as to say that the minister may take over the business, even where he thinks it would fail, without any positive demonstration that this would happen or, in the second place, that he may appoint someone who then becomes an agent, not for the government but for the owner, and who, by that agency, will impose upon the owner the full consequences of whatever he does.
Then, of course, the most serious aspect is that under a broad provision in the bill he is

relieved of any responsibility for what he does. I know objection is taken to the suggestion that these are powers of an extreme nature. But surely this is a power of the most extreme nature. Here is a position where a business may be directed to perform a particular contract, and may then find itself in the position where, if the minister thinks it may likely fail to carry out that contract, he may have a controller appointed. That controller becomes, not the agent of the government, and consequently one who would be in a position where, whatever responsibility the government might have, would carry through to the agent, but he is the agent of the owner. As the agent of the owner he can carry on that business and enter into contracts which may be most detrimental to the future interests of the owner. The owner would be in the position where he could not recover in any way from the agent, as is provided in a subsequent section of the bill.
I suggest that this section is not only something that should not be contemplated, except in an extreme situation, but something which should not be contemplated in any event. The minister made one statement to the effect that there was no difference between the present situation and the situation there would be in an all-out war. I suggest there is one very great distinction, that we are still left under no immediate threat of interference with our ordinary communications. We are not at the present time under any threat that ships which carry supplies to these shores or away from these shores will be interfered with. For all practical purposes we are operating on our normal daily activities in those various occupations in which the people of this country are engaged. I submit that, vitally important as speed may be in defence production, there is nothing in the present state of affairs in this country to justify a power of that kind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
The hon. member has
suggested that there is a difference in the attitude taken in this connection and that taken in connection with defence forces. The difference is that with respect to procurement parliament is to be asked to provide for the fulfilment of a program of about $5 billion over a period of three years, and it is considered that the fulfilment of that program is just as vital as it would be if the program had to be fulfilled during a period of actual war. That is, it is the fulfilment of the program which is considered as the thing which should be done as a deterrent against aggression.
There are many of us who feel that it is just as important to do everything that may

be helpful to deter aggression as it would be to do everything that might be required to win a war, if the attempt to deter the aggression did not succeed.
Now, with respect to defence forces, everything that will be required to build them up to the standard contemplated for the deterring effect will be just as important. The information we have is that that is going to be done by the methods now being employed. It would be only to build up greater forces than those that are now agreed upon as being the proper contribution to this deterring effect that other methods of building up the armed forces would be required. If and when it is felt that the armed forces have to be built up beyond what can be done by the methods presently being followed, other methods will be adopted.
Within those limitations the implementation of the $5 billion program is regarded as quite as important as if there were a fighting war going on. We have the experience of the last war. Many hon. members know that it was necessary to use these powers to overcome the resistance of a former member of parliament who did not want to do his share in his plant of what was required from the particular industry in which he was engaged. It required powers of this kind to compel him to do his part in the production of that particular kindi of goods.
If parliament takes the attitude that it is as important to make this contribution to the deterring effect of this build-up, then I think the methods appropriate to succeed should be available. This is a clause similar to the one to be found in the munitions and supply act, to which recourse was had.
Actions that are taken in the exercise of powers of this kind are quickly known to the public. I am convinced that no such action will be taken that those taking it will not be in position to justify and defend1 in this place. We are meeting now and we are going to meet again and all these actions will be subject to the closest scrutiny and to proper criticism by members of the opposition.
It was necessary to have these powers in order to succeed in the last war, although there were not a great many occasions when they had to be used. It was felt by a former member of this house that they just could not be used, but he finally came around and did his bit as was being done by others in the same industry.
If the suggestion of the hon. member for Kamloops were adopted it would have to be expressed in words that would have the same objectionable feature. It would have to be
Defence Production Act the minister who would exercise discretion as to what part of an enterprise it was necessary to put under a controller. The discretionary power would have to be granted or it would not work. You could not have it left to an outside authority to say that the controller could go to a certain point and no further. It would have to be left to the authority created and empowered by parliament to determine what part it was necessary to control in order to bring about the result. That would imply some discretion, as is covered here, as to whether it would be the whole or part of the business that would be controlled.
The only other words that could be added would be, "or such parts as the minister may feel is necessary for the purpose envisaged", and that would not be any more protection than there is already.

subsubtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I think that there is a possibility of framing an amendment, either along the lines suggested by the Prime Minister or to restrict it to such part as is necessarily occupied with the business. Then the instructions given to a controller would have to be carefully drawn as to whether the whole business, if it were taken over, was necessary to ensure the performance of the work or the compliance with the direction. I do think it is important to have some such limitation in this bill.
With respect to what the Prime Minister has just said, I think this goes beyond what was in the munitions and supply act. Under that act the actions of an investigator were exempt from challenge in the courts, but under this bill the actions of a controller are similarly exempt. Section 36 reads:
No controller or investigator is responsible at law for any act or thing done by him in good faith in the performance of his duties or the exercise of his powers under this act and no action may be taken against a controller or investigator in respect thereof.
After he is appointed no one can question under the bill as it is now drawn whether it was necessary for him to take over all of a plant or to exercise control over it for the length of time which he thinks he should. If he injures the business beyond what is necessary, apart altogether from the compliance with the war contract, no one can hold him responsible.
In view of these circumstances I am convinced that it is necessary to amend the section. It can be amended in a way which will not affect or diminish the power to get war contracts performed but which would preserve the rights of the individual with respect to those parts of his enterprise which

Business of the House are not necessarily connected with the performance of that contract. I believe such an amendment can be drawn and I propose to move one.
Section stands.
Progress reported.
